subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT PETITION TO END CONTROLS ON JUNE 30, 1977
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion now under consideration deals with inflation, the Anti-Inflation Board and the abolition of controls anticipated by the Anti-Inflation Board.
The matter which we are discussing today is not a new one but is rather stale. However the solutions to the problem of inflation are not stale, because this government has apparently not yet found them. Yet, the Anti-Inflation Board was set up by the government specifically to jugulate inflation once and for all. But, Mr. Speaker, try to convince of the AIB's efficiency the housekeeper who goes shopping every week, when the notices that prices go up constantly by 5 to 10 per cent, on an average, every week. Often, all she has to do is lift the price sticker to see last week's and realize the price has gone up by 20 cents on a $2 article. Try to talk to her about the value of the AIB and you will soon hear what she thinks of that bureaucracy which floats in the clouds, putters around with papers and has no clue what is going on in the real world, where things happen.
Before going into the essence of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote an article that goes back to December 14, 1974 and appeared in the newspaper Le Soleil, of Quebec City; it shows just how crazy our economic system is. With supporting figures, we are shown how, with an inflation rate of 10 per cent, which we have known for several years already, a bus ticket worth 40 cents in 1974 will cost $1.15 in 1985, $2.95 in 1995 and $4.70 in the year 2000. It is almost inconceivable, Mr. Speaker, just how savings will be gobbled up, will disappear or depreciate over such a short period of time.
Groceries worth $50 in 1974 will cost $142.65 in 1985. Even now, in 1977, we can readily imagine, if nothing changes, that it will cost $142.65 in 1985. And in the year 2000, it will cost $595.95. A house costing $32,000 in 1974 will cost $85,593 in 1985, and $357,545 in the year 2000. Last night, I heard the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) say that a house now worth $30,000, at a 12 per cent rate of interest, will cost, 12 years later, only in interest, the small amount of $152,000. That is, $152,000 for service charges and interest and $50,000 for the purchase of a house of his choice, that is a $30,000 home.
Mr. Speaker, one of the first measures passed by this government when it was first elected in 1968, has been one to

June 21, 1977

raise the ceiling on interest rates. In 1968, the ceiling was 6Vt to 6'/2 per cent, an average rate in Canada; now, the rate on ordinary loans is 12 per cent. That is why a $30,000 home in 1977 paid off over 30 years will produce an interest of $152,000. To reward financial interests in 1968, we raised the ceiling of interest rates and today, financiers are getting twice as much interest as in 1968. We created inflation, Parliament is responsible and not the provinces, or municipalities or school boards or individuals or unions.
The trade unions fought back because they wanted to survive in that crazy system which was set up by the present government when it suppressed the ceiling on interest rates. Inflation in Canada has been a boon for the present government. Why? Because when a worker earns $200 a week, like we saw last year during the Olympic Games, and when interest rates jump following all those increases in interest rates, to afford a house of his own and all the commodities of life, that worker has to demand twice what he got during the Olympic Games. The federal government, without raising the taxation tables, like the former government of Mr. Bourassa, without raising the taxation tables, increased its budget in ten years from $12 billion to a national budget of almost $50 billion.
That means that inflation has served the present government, because it has worked to its advantage. Without raising taxes, the government has collected more money and taxpayers have paid more tax to the federal and provincial governments. Mr. Speaker, the Anti-Inflation Board was created nearly 24 months ago. During the next few minutes, I should like to emphasize that, firstly, this board has cost a lot of money, secondly, it has hired a great many civil servants and, thirdly, it resulted in a waste of ink and paper by the tons. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, those are the true results of the board's actions. It has spent a lot of money. Some $5,428,000 in 1975-76. Some $12,530,000 in 1976-77. From April to October 1977, it will cost another $7 million. For a grand total of $25 million over a 24-month period, which represents an average of over $1 million a month. Mr. Speaker, the board hired a great many people. In December 1975, it hired 342 employees. In March 1976 and June 1976, it hired 447 and 889 employees respectively.
Between March and June 1976, the Anti-Inflation Board has seen an inflation in the number of its employees which has more than doubled. The number of Anti-Inflation Board employees has reached the imposing figure of 914; but this number does not include the people hired by separate contract. Furthermore, the Anti-Inflation Board has travelled around, since it had to make its presence felt since it could not make its effects felt. That is why it has held hearings in the most expensive hotels in this country while Canadians were faced with prohibitive goods and services costs in Canada because of inflation. My third point, Mr. Speaker, is that the Anti-Inflation Board has produced tons of paper, one of the more concrete results on its part.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on for hours reading releases from the Anti-Inflation Board congratulating itself on its excellent job. In addition to having used a lot of paper, the Anti-Infla-
Anti-Inflation Act
tion Board achieved the following results: It controlled the wages of small wage earners, who were the first victims of inflation, but it did not control the prices paid by the small wage earners. Moreover, it frightened the investors because when they always have a sword over their head they do not invest, and rightly so, because they do not want to risk their capital to produce goods and services when the interest on capital is more productive on bonds which escape or used to escape the controls, than the interest on production capital which can eventually be subject to controls.
Because the investors were afraid, the Anti-Inflation Board has been one of the main causes of the present unemployment. All these results had been forecast by the Social Crediters because we predicted these economic results while the economists hired by the government were showing off the blown-out lantern of the Anti-Inflation Board, following the warnings given by the Social Crediters to the government before the board was established. Others also warned the government about the future inevitable disaster it would encounter with its miracle answer, the establishment of an Anti-Inflation Board. This experience had been tried in the United States when certain price controls were imposed, and it had ended in disaster. The government wanted Canada to repeat this American disaster. In fact, Mr. Speaker, Canada has become an expert in imported American mechanisms which have already failed and which are expected to do miracles in Canada. I well remember as I was in the House in 1962 and 1963, the American nuclear warheads of 1962-63, which are another example of disasters such as the Anti-Inflation Board of 1975.
The Canada Labour Council has published a yellow pamphlet entitled Why met to show that it is the weak who suffer from inflation. It seems that wage controls were established to protect us against inflation. In fact this is a measure which will be detrimental to those who are most affected by inflation: Canadian workers and consumers. Why us? We spend almost all our income for housing, mortgages and food. Those spendings went up by 65, 32 and 49 per cent respectively between 1971 and 1974. We had to face increased obligations whereas our wages averaged 25 per cent more during the same period. Meanwhile higher prices yielded corporate profits exceeding by 111 per cent those of 1971, before the crisis. Why are we the only ones to be blamed? What makes us believe that the government can or wants to control those who are benefiting from inflation?
The guidelines set out in the legislation are full of loopholes allowing accountants to get round such guidelines. Real profits will keep soaring and so will prices. All analysts recognize this fact. Professional fees, land speculation and interest rates are only some of the areas neglected by the legislation. Government spokesmen admitted themselves that inflation would pursue its ravages. Wages are conspicuous and easy to restrict. Therefore the government is going to go for us. Our salaries are going to be restricted but our expenses will go on increasing, not to mention those of the low-income people, of those on fixed wages, of retired people and of those on welfare. They
6942

June 21, 1977
Anti-Inflation Act
are going to be most affected by the government safety measures. We ignored the anti-inflation plan submitted by the Canadian Labour Congress. We substituted to it a program which is both unfair and unworkable. We, as Canadian workers and consumers, are opposed to measures which are directed against us as if we were the source of inflation. Why should we have to pay? Why would we be the only ones to pay the price of inflation?
It was a booklet published by the Labour Council of Canada which demonstrates that, after two years of operation, we were right about the Anti-Inflation Board.
Mr. Speaker, the Anti-Inflation Board has done more harm or bothered more people than it has helped. I wish to give you some examples. In La Presse of January 25, 1977 we can read:

The 25 reporters of the Quotidien of Chicoutimi and Progres-Dimanche have been slowing down their work during the last week to protest against the decision of the Anti-Inflation Board to reduce their salaries negotiated with the employer.
The collective agreement had been accepted by both parties in November 75. It provided weekly salaries of $320 with an increase of $16 on January 1, 1977. The decision of the board freezes the wages at $292 a week.
The situation is the same at Le Nouvelliste of Trois-Rivieres where reporters' salaries have been reduced by $10 to $15 a week and those of publicists by $30 a week.
Mr. Speaker, I have myself known a company in my riding which had reached an agreement with its employees' union but which is still waiting, Mr. Speaker, for a decision by the Anti-Inflation Board allowing the employer to pay the salaries provided in that collective agreement. The employees are still receiving the salaries paid before the collective agreement because the officials of the Anti-Inflation Board have not had time to ratify or study the file of the collective agreement signed by the employer and accepted by the union. That socialist scheme has then been nothing but an impediment to the economic activities in Canada; some press releases of the Anti-Inflation Board were quite ludicrous. On that matter, I wish to refer to the committee sitting of February 8, 1977 when the board announced that 124 Canadian companies had exceeded by $13,055,000 the limit set by the program of the Anti-Inflation Board.
Mr. Speaker, at the time when those 124 companies were blamed for having made a profit of $13 million, they made a big fuss about that discovery, that so-called control. It represents $100,000 per company but if you take into account their gross revenue, their invested capital and their investment needs, an average amount of $100,000 is a real joke.
I will mention only a few of these enterprises which were accused of making profits exceeding $100,000. These are: Alcan Aluminum from Montreal, Canada Cement Lafarge, Quebec Iron and Titanium from Sorel, Avon Products from Dorval, Domtar from Montreal, Northern Telecom from Montreal, Robin Hood Multi-Foods from Montreal, and so on. While 124 Canadian companies had made $13,055,000 in excess profit, 11 Canadian bank institutions were allowed to boost their assets by $30 billion over the last 12 months. If you

review the balance sheets of the banks, you will find that the assets of Canadian banks have shot up by $30 billion in the last twelve months, when the gross national product averages $200 billion in Canada.
That means, Mr. Speaker, that the 11 chartered banks in Canada increased their assets by 15 per cent of the value of the GNP. What did the Anti-Inflation Board do against that outrageous situation? Zilch. It did not get involved with the banks because it is afraid of the sovereign power exercised by the banks now, for the banks have power over the governments they are financing, that power being that of creating money, which was conferred by this federal government, as was the case with previous governments. Small enterprises make a few millions in profit which they have to invest so as to keep their facilities and the economy operating. The Anti-Inflation Board did nothing but bother them with its bureaucracy while the banks were not asked any questions, for they have a sovereign power.
In the monetary field, which they were entrusted with by the federal government, they are allowed to lend 16 times their assets for each dollar deposited in a bank bearing 8 per cent interest to the depositor; in other words, the law permits the banks to extend a credit of $16 at 12 per cent interest, which works out to a gross benefit of 184 per cent of their assets. That explains the $30 billion more in banking assets during the last 12 months in a country whose gross national product is only $200 billion.
One the one hand, Mr. Speaker, businesses are being penalized while on the other they are being asked with the help of Department of Regional Economic Expansion subsidies to invest to create more employment and reduce unemployment and to implement new industries or modernize their operations. Benefits coming out of healthy competition are always reinvested and do automatically create employment because they favour production one way or the other. It is economic madness to penalize their benefits on the one hand while asking them on the other to expand and develop our economy and grant them money to encourage them to invest.
Mr. Speaker, 1 would rather trust statements of experienced businessmen which help out Canada's economic expansion than those of bureaucrat economists who have never run a business. In February 1977, the Chamber of Commerce of London, Ontario, provided the government with an interesting brief based on the following considerations and 1 quote:
We consider the chief causes of inflation to be:
Governments at three levels spending increasing percentages of our gross national product. Their spending in total should not exceed 37'/>
per cent, as stated in our January 1975 statement. Their programs whether statutory (or non-controllable) are not, nor should they be considered to be sacrosanct. They must be limited to come within the 3716 per cent guideline. An individual who spends beyond his or her means enventually goes broke. Likewise our governments, after decades of overspending, are fast going broke.
June 21, 1977

Mr. Speaker, 1 would only want to point out that in my own riding as well as in others, because it must be the same policy, the federal government raised the cost of certain services in the post office by 66% per cent in January. The rental of post office boxes has gone up by 66% per cent in the towns of Granby and Waterloo. The federal government is asking private businesses to limit their increases between 6 and 10 per cent but with respect to its own spendings, its own rates are going up by 66% per cent. I therefore wrote a letter to the Anti-Inflation Board to bring this fact to their attention and I quote:
The following is to bring to your attention an increase of 66Vi per cent that has been put into effect regarding the rental cost of the post office boxes-
-in the riding of Shefford.
Private business must limit the increase in its costs, but the federal government should at least set an example. Such a large increase on the part of a governmental service surely does not help the cause of the fight against inflation.
I then received a letter from one of the civil servants, Mr. Harold A. Renouf, from the Anti-Inflation Board, dated June 16, 1977, and I quote:
1 regret to have to inform you that the charges levied by government services do not come under the Anti-Inflation Board.
Everybody has been put under control, but the government has been exempted!
Nevertheless, I share your opinion that the government should set a good example when it comes to price restraints and it should at least try to explain in details to the public the reasons for those increases when they eventually become necessary.
Mr. Speaker, we are still waiting for those explanations. 1 would like to go on quoting the paper of the Chamber of Commerce of London, Ontario. The second point is as follows: [English]
Money supply increases. Money supply growth must be kept within the inflation rate and productivity increases initially, and gradually reduced to the level of productivity increases.
Wage and salary increases beyond the rate of inflation and productivity growth. Total remuneration packages must not exceed the inflation rate and productivity improvements.
Prices that are undisciplined by competition. We must ensure wherever possible that a healthy level of competition is effective throughout our economy.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think that this is an extremely important point and the Chamber of Commerce of London, Ontario, states on several occasions that when we have healthy competition in business, we automatically have normal prices on the market. We now have an economy where small people are stifled through the Anti-Inflation Board, whereas the big multinationals are left free to operate on an independent basis, as we have seen during the last months and during the last few years. We have only to consider the Canadian situation regarding oil and gas. When, for example, we were paying 50 cents for a gallon of gasoline, the federal government was collecting a much lower sales tax on this gallon than it is doing now on a gallon for which we must pay $1. The main responsibility for inflation rests on the federal government, since it is in its interest to have prices rise to be able to collect
Anti-Inflation Act higher taxes, to increase its expenses and also to have more money to meet its obligations, with the help of inflation.
When the Anti-Inflation Board was set up the Social Credit-ers said that is was going to be a fiasco, that it was going to be a joke, that it would only control little people, that it would not control banks, that it would not control multinational companies. We now know the result of the experiment. In a few days we will be paying at least $1 for a gallon of gas all across Canada. What did the Anti-Inflation Board do? It is all very nice to blame foreign countries, the Arabs, or Canada's oil product suppliers but it is the same thing in all other areas, even products manufactured in Canada because it is in the interest of the government to see salaries rise to produce increased taxes, higher revenues with the deficit budgets that we have had for the past several years.
Mr. Speaker, there would be other extremely interesting remarks to be made about inflation, but as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain suggested earlier, we are relying on the recommendations of economists who propose solutions that were obsolete before they were born. We are still applying solutions, theories that date back over a hundred years. On the one part, we advocate full employment and, on the other hand, we want to increase productivity through modern technology and science, while at the same time seeking to achieve full employment. Those are two contradictory principles in political economy, and there are ministers sitting on the government side who still rely on theories that have been proven to be fiascos. The inflation now was created altogether by an economic system, and particularly a monetary system controlled by multinationals, banks that forced this government and previous governments to give them the exclusive power to control the monetary and financial power in Canada. Wanting to correct inflation in Canada is like flogging a dead horse, unless we deal first with the monetary area, which is the prime cause, particularly since 1968, when this government lifted the interest ceiling on money rates in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Milne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to take part in this debate. I am one member who has expressed some very strong opinions on wage and price guidelines. I was one of those members who campaigned most vigorously against the freeze proposed by the Conservatives in the election campaign of 1974. I also supported the introduction of the wage and price guidelines program in 1975. Tonight I take the position that the program should be continued for some time yet. I will be one member who later this evening will vote against the rather superfluous motion put forward by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens).
I opposed introduction of the wage and price freeze as proposed by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) and the Conservative party in 1974, and I thought for good reason. If the same set of conditions prevailed today I would be just as vigorous in my opposition. If you remember, Mr. Speaker, in

June 21, 1977
Anti-Inflation Act
1974 economic conditions were substantially different from the present day. The economy was short of goods, it was short of manpower, and it was short of money.
Not true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: In terms of wanting to increase supply you had to produce more. If the hon. member for Halifax and the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies), who I understand was the author of that program, had had their way certainly it would have been the most devastating thing that could have happened not only to the economy but to the small business community.
How could we be worse off than we are today with one million unemployed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
At that time world food prices were rising. The world price for oil was going up by four. Industrial materials were increasing substantially in price. At that point in time a freeze would, in my opinion, have been very wrong. The problem was supply, with too many dollars chasing too few goods.
In 1975 conditions changed. I think hon. members on the other side should open their eyes. If they were in a situation where they went to a doctor with some kind of health problem one year and the doctor prescribed some kind of remedy and they went back a year or so later with a different problem, surely they would expect the doctor to view it differently. Hon. members opposite seem to have a one track mind on this thing; they wanted a solution that would answer all types of situations in the economy. In spite of the reputation of the hon. member for Don Valley as an economist, they are surely not being very realistic.
I supported the program that was introduced in 1975 for a number of reasons. There had been a downturn in the economy of many industrial countries in the world. We were experiencing, as the minister and a number of members on this side have said strongly, a period of inflation resulting from a psychological base where people expected and wanted more in anticipation of the future. But the fundamental reason I supported the program in 1975, and why I am going to vote to continue it tonight, is simply that the country cannot afford to lose its relativity in the export market, particularly the United States.
1 think that is extremely important. Many members on both sides of the House have said we need to take a serious look at the structure of our economy, but in my opinion there has not been any meaningful or significant dialogue in that area. Therefore I think controls should remain until we have had the opportunity to do so.
As I have said, I will be voting against the motion. Prior to doing that may I say I have spent a fair amount of time surveying my constituents. The whole purpose of the government's publishing the book "The Way Ahead" was to initiate dialogue, and I chose to use it with various groups in my constituency. I want to put on the public record of this place that the business community, as represented in the city of

Brampton by the Board of Trade, took my invitation seriously and held discussions on its contents. They surveyed their entire membership and reported back to me. I met with them to review the results of their survey amongst their membership, and fully two thirds of the business community of Brampton are opposed to the lifting of wage and price guidelines at this time.
As a matter of fact, a good half of the remaining one third said that they were in favour of lifting the program, but they qualified their answers. They said they would be in favour of removing the program at this time if there were a follow up agency which essentially had the same type of power; or that they would be in favour of lifting the program if they could be sure that inflation would not return or if they were satisfied that labour rates would remain more or less constant. If you interpret that as a qualified answer, you could certainly say that well over three quarters of the respondents in the business community of my city want me to stand here and say that they are opposed to the removal of this program at this point in time.
I represent a riding with a high percentage of secondary industry. Many industries in my riding are in the secondary manufacturing sector and rely heavily on exports of their manufactured products, mostly to the United States. Many people charged with the management of these plants have been to see me to express the deep concern they have as to how competitive they are. They realize that some of their customers are not buying as much as they traditionally have but, more important, they are really concerned as to whether or not they can compete in the market.
If we decided to be opportunists like the hon. member for York-Simcoe would like the House to be, and lift the controls immediately perhaps there would be some short term applause. But I will wager a fair amount that members on the opposite side would be on their feet in the question period within a week or two demanding that something be done to improve exports. 1 cannot think of anything more constructive that we could do in the long term than continue the anti-inflation program.
1 have all kinds of representations from the business community I represent. On one hand they indicate we should have a higher tariff structure so that more products are not coming in, and on the other we should be financing and subsidizing industry a good deal more for them to be able to compete in the export market. That is just the same as a dog going around biting its own tail. There is no way to win in a situation like that. While it may be rather unpalatable in the short term, will cause some dislocation and will cause some levelled off expec-tions, to give up our position in the export market is disastrous for the industrial sector of this country and therefore the employment sector. There are certain groups in our society who want us to terminate the program as of now, or very soon.
I think it is worth toughing it a bit longer so that we will have that long term gain.

June 21, 1977

1 represent a riding in which there is a high degree of construction. There are few other ridings in Canada where residential construction is as high as it is in the city of Brampton, or indeed, that there is as much commercial and industrial construction as there is in that area. One of the real causes of our inflation two or three years ago was the very high wage settlements that were obtained in the construction industry. The result of this was that in the short construction season builders were almost willing to pay any kind of settlement in order to have some labour peace during the construction season and to get on with their building.
One of the problems we are faced with in this country is the fact that companies are starting to say that they can build their plants in the States rather than in Canada, because they can get lower labour rates down there than they can in Canada. That is of concern because we are already giving up two of the greatest advantages this country has had, a labour rate that has been marginally lower than the United States and the fact that we have had a large quantity of low cost natural resources. Both of those points are not as much in our favour as they used to be.
You cannot expect some person in the labour force to be as happy with the same wage level here in Canada as he might be on the States side. Elis personal cost of living is higher in this country. One thing which makes it higher is the high cost of housing. It is impossible to buy any type of shelter in Brampton for under $50,000. It is not difficult to have a very modest home and pay $70,000. On the other side of the border, perhaps housing costs are not much more than half or two thirds of that. There is a lot of vested interest in terms of trying to get some of our construction costs down by playing it cool, and doing that by the continuation of the program.
I accepted an invitation from a large labour organization in my riding to go and discuss the whole anti-inflation program with them. It was a most interesting evening. They presented me with a very substantial brief. The content of that brief was similar to that which Mr. Morris presented to the government on behalf of the entire labour movement. Essentially they were making the point in that brief that there were three things they felt were fundamental to improving the economy of the country at this time.
They felt the number one problem we are dealing with is unemployment. The most significant way to deal with unemployment would be to remove the controls immediately. Their second point was that it was of vital concern to them that the housing program should be more vigorous than it is at the present time. Their third point was, rather than the budget giving some assistance to the business community to invest and expand, that those dollars should have gone into direct tax cuts and should have been accompanied by a substantial cut in personal taxes, as well as a government subsidy from the federal level to the municipal and provincial levels so that they in turn could reduce their taxes.
I think that is the fundamental problem facing the country. On the one hand we have the business community saying that the controls should remain. They are concerned about an
Anti-Inflation Act
upsurge in inflation, labour rates, and our role in the export market. The leadership of the labour community feel very strongly that the controls program should be removed immediately to address the problem of unemployment. Certainly the polls and surveys do not indicate that all the people who belong to the labour movement necessarily feel the same. Until we get some kind of a resolution or a meeting of minds, we have no other alternative but to continue the program for a period of time.
I am not sure either group would appreciate me saying this, but in some ways both groups were taking their positions for the wrong reasons. Some of the business community want the controls program to continue for a period of time so that they can have a lever on the labour rates they are obliged to pay. The labour group want the controls program to end, although they were very careful to say they wanted it to continue on the price side and not on the wage side. They wanted that so that they can tackle their unemployment situation and try to gain back those wage gains which they were obligated to give up because of the guidelines set up by the AIB and that part of the increase more particularly that was rolled back by the Anti-Inflation Board.
Yesterday, and a few times previous to that, the leaders of the business community and the leaders of the labour movement met with government, which puts us in an encouraging position. While there has been no meeting of minds on any real, firm commitments, by virtue of the answer given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) today, the dialogue is coming closer and both sides are starting to see they have a mutual interest in solving this problem rather than taking diametrically opposed positions.
I met with the labour organization in Brampton. Obviously all of them did not agree, but I attempted to put the thesis to them that I thought controlling inflation was probably the most effective thing we could do to improve the employment situation. If we were to get out of the program in the short term and ignore inflation, in a year or so there would probably be a substantial lift in the economy; but perhaps four or five years down the road this would not work in their best interests and would not be in the best interests of the labour movement. We cannot continue to price ourselves out of the export market and out of our own domestic market, because one of the difficulties we have in this country is trying to compete for the domestic market against countries which can produce and come in over the top of our rather substantial tariff walls and still compete more than successfully in our domestic markets.
I want to say as sincerely as I can to the people in my constituency who belong to the labour movement that 1 do not in any way, shape or form downgrade or not take seriously the level of unemployment. Generally speaking, I represent one of the richer areas of Canada. When parliament, the newspapers and others were talking about unemployment, they were generally not talking about the city of Brampton and that part of the Golden Horseshoe surrounding the city of Toronto. This unemployment was generally in the maritimes, part of Quebec, northern Ontario and so on.

At the present time the unemployment rate in Brampton is as high or higher than it has ever been because secondary manufacturing is an area which has been hit. Before it was always a big paper plant that was shut down, but this time it is smaller plants that have difficulties exporting. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
I argue on the opposite side. I presume the hon. member for Don Valley has his name on Mr. Speaker's list. I will listen to his argument in support of lifting the controls, but I sincerely say to him and to the House that I take the opposite point of view because, without them, we would go back to high inflation in short term, and that would be in the worst interests of the people whom we try to help.
In terms of unemployment, we should take a careful look at the situation. It has been announced recently that unemployment is in the order of 8 per cent. That seems very high, and it is high, but when you analyse it further you find that there are some significant facts and figures within that statistic which should go on the record.
First of all, the last Statistics Canada figures indicate that the unemployment rate is now 7.9 per cent, down from 8.3 per cent, a substantial drop of some .6 per cent. 1 do not hear any members in the House, particularly on the opposition front bench, or the hon. member for York Simcoe, commenting on that. When unemployment goes up .5 per cent he is on his feet shouting what a disaster that is, but when it drops .6 per cent it seems to escape his notice.
When you look at the employment situation you find that the number of households that have no wage earner at all is less than one in four of those listing unemployment. In other words, when there is someone in the household who is unemployed, only one in four of those households does not have at least one or more wage earners earning income for that home. This has helped to soften the situation, making it less drastic than the 8 per cent would indicate.
There has been a very high entry into the work force, in spite of the fact that our economy has increased to provide a substantial increase in the number of job establishments. The problem really is the high entry rate. The high entry rate has been extremely high among females between the ages of 25 and 44. I certainly understand why so many of them are entering the work force. They are simply doing it because the cost of housing, the cost of food, and the cost of so many things that families buy these days has gone up so much that they need more than one income in the home to be able to maintain the standard of living they have, or indeed to begin to approach the standard of living they would like. 1 cannot think of anything that would help correct that situation any more than to control inflation the best we can.

I want to conclude by making a couple of other points. The point I was trying to make is that while unemployment is high and while, I am sure, every member of the House is concerned about it-I am particularly sensitive to it as it applies to my constituents-we now belong to a society where there is a multiple pay cheque in many households, and three out of four of the households where someone is unemployed do have someone in the labour force, and almost one in three have two or more people in the work force, in spite of the fact they may have one or more who are unemployed.
One of the comments that has been made very often by people discussing the AIB program-certainly to me in letters and conversation-is that the program is not fair on the basis that the cost of many of the things on which money is spent is not controlled. They speak about electrical energy, energy of all types, municipal taxation, and food. 1 would like to make a few comments on the food industry.
I think it is fair to say-as a matter of fact the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has said it on one or more occasions-that the results of the program have been materially assisted by the fact that last year the price of food came down. One of the reasons that our performance under the AIB is not as good this year as it was last year has been the resurgence in the price of food. I support that resurgence because I have many constituents, friends and acquaintances, who are primary producers, and there are many farmers across this country who have lost thousands and thousands of dollars in the beef business. Unless they have some kind of relief by having the consumer pay a higher price for that product-and we hope there is a flow through to the farmer-we will be in a situation of having many producers out of business and, I venture to say, the price will double in a year or two because there will be a scarcity of beef. The same is true with pork.
I appeal to Canadians to accept the fact that, while they read in the paper of the excess profits that many of the food processors are making, there are substantial number of primary producers, particularly in the beef sector, who have suffered badly.
I want to congratulate the government on some moves it has made in the last little while that have been beneficial to the farm community. I think one of them has been the exemption of family farms from capital gains tax. Along with the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) I petitioned the Minister of Finance prior to the present budget to have the proceeds from the sale of land that is reinvested in land escape capital gains tax. This view was shared by most members who represent the farming community.
There is one more step that the Minister of Finance should take in this area, that is, that when a farm is incorporated for a variety of reasons, that it be allowed to roll over taxes on the same basis as an a non-incorporated farm. I have argued a number of times that only the land portion of the incorporation should have that advantage-I do not think the associated businesses should have it. Nevertheless, I want to make a couple of comments and to congratulate the government again

on publishing a statement on food policy, as it did a few days ago.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Hon. members can take it lightly, as does the hon. member for Don Valley, who probably does not have many cows in his region or who has not cleaned many stables.
A proper food policy-1 am convinced that the document sets out the basic strategy for it-is in the best interests of both the producer and the consumer. Somehow most hon. members on the other side, and many other people, cannot seem to understand that a good food policy is in the best interests of both producer and consumer. Many people take the point of view that it is either to the advantage of the producer or it is a cheap food policy for the consumer, but in fact it is not. And I endorse the basic principles that are set out that we should support marketing boards, that we should have a good program of income stability, that we need to be sensitive on a short term basis in our tariff policy, and that farmers, because they deal with unpredictable situations such as weather, should have a good program of crop insurance available to them at rates they can afford.
As to marketing boards, they have drawn a lot of comments from many people. There are hon. members on the other side who take the position they want nothing to do with marketing boards, but that the government should be there.
Talk to your Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Horner) about that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
I was on a platform with our new minister last Saturday, and 1 should point out to the hon. member opposite who is interjecting that the minister stood up and explained this policy. As a matter of fact he enunciated it very well indeed.
Hon. members opposite talk about how bad marketing boards are, but I do not see them standing up and introducing motions saying we should do away with the Canadian Wheat Board.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Don't lecture me. Lecture the Minister without Portfolio.

There is a good deal of concern among farmers at the present time as to the future of marketing boards. This is reflected by many of the discussions in this House and in our committees. Whether the government is committed to marketing boards or not is being discussed. I want to tell hon. members that years ago I worked in the agricultural industry. 1 had a lot to do with the poultry business. 1 worked with farmers who had very large flocks of laying hens, and with farmers who were involved in the production of meat birds. 1 have seen some of the best farms in Ontario, which had been owned for two and three generations, turned over to feed companies.

Look at some of your ministers and you will feel more humiliated.

At one time farmers had high volumes of product and extremely low prices. That drove producers out of business. When there was a scarcity prices were high, and it was always the small, genuine farmer who got hurt in that situation. The thing marketing boards have done, particularly in the poultry industry which is easy to get into on a short-term has been to bring stability. As a matter of fundamental policy 1 think the government should do everything it can to make us as self sufficient in energy, housing and food production as possible, and certainly one of the fundamental-

Mr. Speaker,
1 rise to speak in the controls debate this evening without any apology for the position of the Conservative party in 1974, and to remind hon. members present that had this party won that election the controls would have ended more than two and a half years ago.
Hear, hear!

This debate would have been history. During that election campaign hon. members opposite tried to make 90 days seem like forever, but 90 days is a far shorter time than the time we have lived through this controls program already. I suppose one of the main reasons 1 rose tonight is that I was prodded by the remarks of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) the other evening, and again by the remarks made this evening by the hon. member for Peel-Duff-erin-Simcoe (Mr. Milne). Both those hon. members are marvellous revisionists. They are re-writers of history, but I remind them that it takes at least three decades for a revisionist to write with any credibility at all. To try to revise history after less than three years is an exercise, while carried out with a straight face by the hon. members opposite, that is not going to fool the opposition nor the public.

June 21, 1977
Anti-Inflation Act
For the hon. member for Davenport to suggest, as he did the other evening, that during that campaign the difference between the Tories and the Liberals was a matter of judgment as to when to bring in controls and as to when they were necessary, is absolutely laughable. When one remembers the ridicule and the scorn which were poured on the policy presented by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), then the leader of this party, on platform after platform across this country, it is difficult to believe that anybody could present such a picture of what it was all about three years ago in this House after such a short time, and claim to have any credibility at all. I remind the hon. member for Davenport that a week and a half ago he was pleading in this House for hon. members to have some faith in what he said and to believe him. For him a week later to make a statement with no shred of truth in it, 1 find it an amazing thing.
We know that the Liberal opposition to controls at the time of the 1974 election campaign was total. The candidate who ran for the Liberal party against me said that the whole idea of any kind of controls was foreign to his party, that its members could never bring themselves to it and that it was against every principle they upheld. It is astonishing to hear the speeches and the thread of thought of the two hon. members I mentioned, and of many more in the course of this debate.
It was interesting too that we were told in 1974 that any attempt at control, either in Britain or in the United States, had failed. I was sharply reminded of that a few months ago when a constituent sent to me an essay by Robert Lekachman entitled "The Specter of Full Employment", found in Harper's Magazine which described the American attempt at controls. Part of the essay reads as follows:
Nixon preached the wickedness of interference with private markets, but nevertheless suddenly froze prices August 15, 1971, and followed the ninety-day freeze with a year or so of more flexible but astonishingly successful wage- and price-hike limitations.
Nowhere in 1974 could one find a quote like that in any literature. Oh, to have found that one during that 1974 campaign! It would have been worth a couple of thousand votes to have found somebody with the courage to have made that assessment of a 90-day freeze and then a gradual withdrawal and a phasing out of controls.
We must remember too the embarrassment of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) as he struggles with this method of controlling which has been imposed by the Liberal government. It was not too long ago that the former minister of finance, the former member for Ottawa-Carleton, left this House because he could not bear the thought of having to try to explain away and pilot through a controls program in this House.
The former member for Ottawa-Carleton always wanted to look good, but there is no way to make the government and the Minister of Finance look good in their endeavour to make the controls program work. It does not matter how sweetly they sing the tune. I am reminded of an old folk song that the balladeers sing. Sometimes they do it seriously, and sometimes

they do it as a burlesque. I think we have been hearing the burlesque part of it. That old song has in it lines about a cherry that had no stone, a chicken that had no bone, and a story that had no end. That line about the cherry that had no stone is pretty appropriate. I am not really implying that the government is rotten to the core, but 1 am certainly suggesting that the controls program was not firm at the core and that it ailed from its foundation. The public was very swiftly aware of that. The problem was the exception: the Crown corporations, the Post Office, companies with limited employment, and commercial rents.
The government has excepted.

Food prices did not seem to matter at all. I am sure hon. members opposite had constituents, as 1 did, who did a marvellous job of watch-dogging prices. Some constituents sent me itemized day by day accounts of price increases after the imposition of the controls program. That information was passed on to the AIB. Phone calls were made. These constituents received phone calls, were thanked for their effort, and that was about it. They quickly realized that it did not make any sense to monitor prices like that because there was no way that the Anti-Inflation Board was going to tackle prices with anything like the same vigour it tackled some aspects of wages.
As far as the chicken that had no bone is concerned, the program is firm in all the wrong places and predictably soft in other places. It is an example of gross inequities. In my constituency those inequities were felt very sharply. About a year ago there was a strike by coal miners in the east part of Okanagan-Kootenay against the Anti-Inflation Board because of a settlement that had been mutually worked out with the company. Fortunately the company was in a profitable position because it had renegotiated its prices with Japan. The workers were aware of the change, yet their settlement was rolled back. They sent a delegation to Ottawa. They went on strike. They stayed out far too long, it seems to me, particularly when the jurisdiction of the board was being reconsidered. The board stood firm, however. I will get back to that company, Mr. Speaker, because of another matter which came up recently.
Then we had the example of the B.C. Teachers' Federation. Compulsory abitration, binding on both sides, had been imposed by law many years ago. Those arbitration boards met in the fall of 1975 and there was nothing in the provincial law at all to direct them to the Anti-Inflation Board. There was no clear indication of whether it had jurisdiction over them and their activities proscribed originally by law, so they brought down a legally binding settlement that had to be accepted by the school boards and teachers. Those settlements were eventually referred to the Anti-Inflation Board by the Minister of Education in the province.
I wrote to that minister and advised him that he should not lightly overturn the principle of arbitration under which teach-
June 21, 1977

ers' salaries had been settled in British Columbia for years and years. However, he did turn them over to the Anti-Inflation Board. At the same time representatives from the government of British Columbia were here in Ottawa arguing against the jurisdiction being extended to the province of British Columbia. The cases in the court are not settled yet.
I do not know why the Anti-Inflation Board, when it received that reference, did not simply quote British Columbia law and say the jurisdiction had not been settled and that it had no power. Instead, it got involved in the game of rollback and again it became fearfully complicated. It is not finished yet. It defies the imagination, Mr. Speaker.
When the minister was asked the question raised so eloquently in the House last week by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) about the very large increases given to company executives, the Minister of Finance, replying on behalf of the AIB and the controls program, said that some of those increases concerned contracts which had been entered into prior to the program. That goes a long way back but increases are only becoming apparent now. One would wonder why the same reasoning has not been applied to the B.C. Teachers' Federation when their increases were rolled back.
An interesting thing about the executive pay increases is that they involve an executive of the coal company which had made a joint presentation with the miners to the Anti-Inflation Board. It would be very difficult now for me to go back to those miners and try to persuade them that this program had worked well and had been equitable. They could hardly see it as anything but the roughest kind of justice. There was no backbone at all in the fight against prices, so the second line of the song is true.
1 think one of the lines that should concern us most is "a story that had no end." After listening to the Minister of Finance and hon. members opposite who have had such a change of heart since 1974, it seems that the controls program will "have no end" as long as they are in power.
We must give credit to the hon. member for Qu'Appel le-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) who saw all this so clearly during the original debate on the controls program and voted against the bill on second reading to make the point that he feared the tendency of the government to extend power to the bureaucracy. As we listen to the debate we are reminded of his comments and how accurate they were.
The program has not really worked, Mr. Speaker. It is building in perpetual inflation. It sets limits that are accepted too readily by companies, and probably accepted too readily by workers who joined in this business of destroying the competitive position of industry.
The hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe apologized for the lack of competition in Canada. It is just the result of Liberal policies over the last 20 years, Mr. Speaker,-an astonishing display of crocodile tears as he spoke of how badly the competitive position of Canadian industry has been eroded in recent years.
Anti-Inflation Act
The governement is still absolutely rapacious in taxation. We have as evidence the new taxes on the life insurance industry. By and large the public is not even aware of what is about to be taken away from them, and still hope to cash in policies they have held for a long time. There is an appalling shift of policy here, Mr. Speaker.
The government has not shown restraint itself. Through a variety of programs it has shown there is almost a limitless fund of money which it has moved around programs like the Local Initiatives Program, Canada Works, Young Canada Works-the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) apparently can always come up with another $100 million for another program.
A year ago we could not even afford a party on July 1. There was such restraint that there was not $500,000-not $100,000-not even ten cents to let off a firecracker. One wonders why suddenly this year there is $3'/' million to celebrate Dominion Day, although they do not want to call it that. Most of the $3Vi million is not going into fireworks but is going into brainwashing the Canadian people so that the name can be changed to Canada Day. This campaign has been launched under the guise of making a truly great celebration this year. If ever there was need of a celebration it was a year ago, but the government's timing is just as bad on this as on other issues.
The government is faced with an enormous credibility problem. Who can believe it? Who can accept its promises? I know there are some voices in the public saying that controls should remain; that is to be expected. It is a sort of "Prisoner of Chillon" syndrome that eventually the chains and walls become attractive. It means passing the load to the government or the AIB rather than fighting it out at the local level.
There is some fear around, because nobody knows what the government will do next after what it did when the 1974 election was over. Of course the program was ailing from the beginning because there was no mandate. If the Minister of Finance had reported to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that the situation was out of control and the government's methods for combating inflation ineffective, the prime Minister should have announced his resignation and that of his government, because it had no mandate to do what it did on October 15, 1975. By imposing controls, contrary to what it had said in the election campaign, the government betrayed the Canadian people. Every time the hon. member for Halifax rises to speak in this House it reminds me of that day of infamy.
One suspects that the controls program is being maintained because the government is not yet ready to announce that it has made some kind of agreement with the Canadian Labour Congress. Mr. Speaker, the $10 million the government made available in that regard shocked some elements of the business community who know they were treated over the years as a source of revenue and were not considered for subsidies. One need not tell them to what use that fund will be put.

Remember, the Canadian Labour Congress passed a resolution calling for a one day national protest strike. That strike did not give a clear answer, for it neither worked well enough nor failed badly enough. Since that day of protest gave no clear-cut answers, the negotiations continued. At present the government wants to involve labour and business in a tripartite system or council which will advise in the running of the country. The government, or the bureaucracy, prefers that system to returning to the freer exchange of ideas to which we were accustomed before the controls program began, or to adopting what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) proposed the other day in his speech on controls.
If the controls program extends to next spring, some 70 per cent of corporations will be locked into agreements, and some 50 per cent of all pay contracts will also be locked into agreements, and we shall see a period of relative peace between labour and industry. That will enable the government to campaign on the issue of national unity and ignore wage and price controls; for it is the great fear of the government that, if the people remember what happened in the 1974 election campaign, it may have to sell them the controls program. One knows the government would not dare go to the people and attempt to sell this program, not after the way it has worked these many months. Therefore the government will pretend that it has worked out some formula which will buy labour peace, at the price of democracy, particularly parliamentary democracy, and it will proclaim and advertise that program all over the country.
Suddenly those members who rose in their place to defend controls will not find anything good to say about the controls program, will claim it had to end on such and such a date, and will announce in its place the great, shining dream of industrial peace, security and safety. The government will campaign on national unity, and the Prime Minister will conduct a phony compaign along lines developed by himself against the premier of the province of Quebec. When 1 say this 1 think of the Prime Minister addressing that audience on the prairies and telling the people they are being "conned" by the premier of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, one thing is certain: If the premier of Quebec conned anybody in Canada, he learned from that consummate master, the Prime Minister.
Therefore I willingly stand up to say it is time controls ended, that unemployment is grim indeed, that business increasingly lacks confidence in the economy, that unemployment is rising ever higher and inflation is far from defeated, as anyone who goes shopping knows. The security the controls program promised is not the security on which one should rely. The government's program is different indeed from the program the Conservatives advocated in 1974.
I know the controls program in force since 1975 is not the program we presented. Ours would have finished by the time this one started, and conditions in this country in terms of inflation and unemployment would have been better than the sorry picture we now see.

Mr. Speaker, other members have said many of the things I wanted to say,

perhaps better than I could have said them. I am pleased to participate briefly in the present debate, which is timely and on a subject which has affected each and every Canadian for the past 20 months, and for some time before that.
Having listened to the financial critic of the opposition, 1 felt he did not make his case in support of the motion before the House which calls for controls to end at the end of this month. Certainly the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) and other hon. members opposite and on my side of the House made good contributions in a timely debate, conducted at a high level.
I submit the controls program this government introduced some 20 months ago has worked well, and that fact has disturbed hon. members opposite deeply.
Tell us, how did it work well?

The government's program is considerably different-and hon. members are still confused on the point- from the freeze program the Conservative party advocated in the 1974 election campaign. The Canadian electorate, incidentally, rejected their program. The program this government implemented, reluctantly, in October, 1975, was of a different kind and embodied an approach different from that embodied in the program to which the electorate said no in July, 1974.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: It is devastatingly different.

That is right, it is devastatingly different. It has succeeded, which disturbs hon. members opposite. Experience has shown that the government's controls program was timely and basically different in concept from the proposal put forward by the Conservatives in the last election campaign.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Yes, it was different, just as the metric system is different.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on behalf of the many people in my province and constituency who are unorganized and, in essence, unprotected from the ravages of inflation. By those two terms I do not mean only the pensioners and those on fixed incomes, what we might call the poor class of society. I certainly include in the unprotected and the unorganized both the small businessman and the farmer. Often they are not necessarily poor. However, they would like to see this control program remain for a period of time until there is greater evidence of responsibility by labour and big business that we will not again be looking at the same kind of inflation balloon.
During this debate someone said that this program legislates inflation by setting out limits, guidelines, and so on. It is true in that sense. The limits become the minimum on one hand and the maximum on the other. In essence we are legislating inflation at a regulated level. Surely that is a good deal better than what we had before the introduction of the program.
June 21, 1977

The hon. member for Okanagan Kootenay (Mr. Johnston) made a fairly good case, pointing out the many inequities that have come about as a result of the application of this program. The fact is that it did interfere with what had come to be accepted bargaining processes, not only in British Columbia in teacher collective bargaining but in other areas of collective bargaining. Certainly there were rollbacks. In many cases there should have been rollbacks.
There is no doubt that there have been injustices in the application of the program. However, there were greater injustices before the program was introduced. Certainly there are far fewer injustices since the inception of the program than if the government had stood back and done nothing in that period of time. Injustices were rampant before the program was introduced.
I want to review briefly Canada's position in so far as other countries are concerned with regard to its fight against inflation. When you look at the figures for the 24 OECD nations you see that Canada has the eighth lowest rate of inflation. Some members say we should be doing better than that. Our economy is perhaps more sensitive to external fluctuation than most others. Therefore it is indeed a remarkable achievement to be eighth among the 24 member countries.
I do not believe there is any other country similarly tied to world trade that can boast of an inflation rate that is near our present rate of 7.6 per cent. Indeed were it not for price rises in imported goods, mainly food products such as coffee, tea, and vegetables, our rate would be below 7 per cent. The estimate is 6.7 per cent. 1 am sure hon. members will agree that 6.7 per cent is not very far off the government's second year goal for this program of getting inflation down to about 6 per cent.
There is still a challenge on the part of the government and all Canadians to try to bring the consumer price down further. Leaving the controls on for a longer period will allow this country to realize more quickly our goal, than by throwing out controls at the beginning of next month. The fact that we still face a rising cost of living index is sufficient to warrant a continuation of wage and price controls. There are other reasons for continuing this program for some period of time.
I hope members opposite will realize during the course of this debate that to adopt their approach and throw out controls at this time would be to give up some of the ground that has been gained. I say that not so much in terms of reducing price increases and a levelling of profits and wage increases, but in terms of the realization that seems to be developing, albeit too slowly to suit many of us, that we are getting a more responsible kind of attitude on the part of labour and big business. We have a further distance to go before most Canadians in my part of the country will agree they have learned their lesson and are prepared to follow it as far as open season is concerned for the average Canadian.
One of the major problems that forced the government to implement guidelines was a very rapid rate of inflation fueled by many areas within our economy. Labour costs and prices were running in circles. Prices were rising. There were settle-
Anti-Inflation Act
ments of 25 and 30 per cent, and demands for a great deal more. Obviously that kind of situation could not continue.
A further indication of the benefit of controls is apparent when one compares the rise in wages to contract settlements over the past couple of years. In 1975 the average settlement by contract was around 20 per cent. Hon. members realize that kind of average level of increase could not continue without repercussions, not only here in Canada but internationally, in so far as trade is such an important part of Canadian life. Already we are paying the price for some of those increases.
Following the introduction of price and wage guidelines in 1975, the situation began to change for the better. By the end of the first quarter of 1976, contract settlements dropped to the area of 15 per cent. As I say, it appears that we are making some progress in that sense.
Canadians deserve some congratulations. Without the support of the great majority of working people and small businessmen in this country over the past year and a half, we would not have had any success with this program. The achievement of bringing down the rate of increase of profits and wages was not secured without considerable restraint on the part of a great number of Canadians.
The achievements of this restraint psychology are also shown in the tremendous improvement in Canada's strike record. A couple of years ago none of us were proud of the number of manhours lost in this country due to strikes. In the first quarter of this year British Columbia was down by about 87 per cent in terms of the number of manhours lost by strikes compared with a couple of years ago.
The advantage of having the country's economy subject to fewer slowdowns and walkouts is obvious to everyone. These important figures indicate that the atmosphere in which labour negotiating is occurring today is a good deal healthier than it was a year ago. I say again that we need to improve that atmosphere considerably before we can afford to let go the wage and price controls.
Members opposite still accuse the government of failing to protect citizens from massive increases in prices. That is not true either, because the Anti-Inflation Board through its recent figures indicates it has forced some 461 firms to return almost $100 million in excess revenues to their customers or clients. In that sense the argument we hear so often from the NDP that business has not been forced to comply with the guidelines and principles is not borne out by the figures. The A1B has made 44 food processing firms give 30 days notice of selected price increases. This requirement to notify of price increases has been another positive feature of the program.
I do not think the country is yet ready for the lifting of controls. I would, of course, like to see us get out of this particular program, as far as that goes. But we did not have any pattern of policies for dealing with a high level of inflation and a high level of unemployment. The construction industry-
