Anti-Inflation Act

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: The construction industry wants controls lifted right away.

I have no doubt about that. In that industry, instead of three or four year contracts for which they were bargaining before controls, they are now down to bargaining on a one-year basis, so they will be ready when controls come off to jump in and look for a larger increase. It is very debatable. The hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis) can argue the case if he likes, but suppose controls were to come off tomorrow, how much more activity would take place within that industry? I believe that before we saw an increase in construction we would see a major increase in inflation.
How did you campaign in 1974?

I campaigned in 1974 in opposition to the freeze policy advanced by the former leader of the opposition. I supported wholeheartedly the government's stand in opposing the freeze advocated by the hon. member for Halifax. We were unable at that time to learn of any plans the Conservative party had beyond the 90-day freeze. I have listened to hon. members speak in this debate, as I have listened to them for the past year and a half, and I have yet to hear any concrete suggestion which goes beyond that 90-day freeze. Surely, the experience of the western cattle raisers with respect to the freeze on beef prices is a sufficient lesson. They do not need to be reminded of the effects of a 90-day freeze with no follow-up.
I do not think there is any region in Canada which is more vulnerable to inflation than is western Canada, or, to be more specific, the province of Saskatchewan with its economy based on agriculture. The prices we get for our products are determined primarily by international markets, yet our cost of production is directly affected by the rate of inflation both domestically and outside this country. The people of Saskatchewan want no part of another round of inflation. Indeed they are not happy about the present level of inflation.
The business community does not want controls thrown out of the window, yet that is what the opposition is really proposing today. It is true that some union leaders continue to oppose the program and I am sure they do so sincerely, even though selfishly in my view. They have even convinced the premier of Saskatchewan to reverse his position. The government of Saskatchewan, along with others, was advocating some kind of controls program; it was only a year or so later that the premier of the province, along with the premier of Manitoba, who had urged the federal government to act, reversed their stand on controls. It is my feeling that if you spoke to the premier of Saskatchewan privately he would say, despite the difficulties in his own party, that his first reaction was the right one and that controls ought to be left in place for some time yet.
The great majority of the people of Saskatchewan, regardless of their status in life, do not want controls lifted. Sure, they would like to make changes; they would like to see the economy operating in such a way as to make controls unneces-

sary. But all working Canadians have pretty well demonstrated their feelings on the issue as can be gathered from the kind of support they have given the program. Without the support of a whole host of people the program would not have worked. Hon. members opposite seem to forget that the Canadian people support controls.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said not long ago in Montreal that although he would scrap the AIB he would give almost identical power to the cabinet or to some agency or department such as the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Well, it is hard, while calling for an end to the Board, to argue in favour of the program in another form. I am not sure whether the hon. gentleman has really thought that one out.
The people in my constituency are not yet convinced that either big business or big labour is really ready to show a more responsible approach to bargaining or to price setting, an approach which balances their own objectives against a measure of public responsibility. Certainly we need changes. We need changes in bargaining legislation. We need changes in the operation of the competition legislation. I was pleased to read the remarks of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) in the debate yesterday spelling out some of the changes which are necessary in these areas.
When we can convince the public that there is a will on the part of organized labour to curb its tendencies to self-interest-some will call it greed-and procedures to accompany it, we shall be in a position to move fairly fast to phase out controls. Parliament itself should be convinced that it will not mean another expensive round of inflation and that the poor and unprotected will not once again be, as it were, in open season for big business and big labour. Further evidence is yet required that there is an adequate change of heart or attitude on the part of those involved. For these reasons I urge the minister to plan the phasing out of controls, but to do so slowly, bearing in mind the considerations I have mentioned.
There has been discussion about a consultative forum involving labour, business, and government. Those discussions have gone on for many years in different forms, with different variations in the concept. I hope that they are successful. I think that the chance of their being successful today is perhaps a bit greater than it has been over the last number of years.
The question then arises as to what kind of authority or what kind of power such a group should have, if any. I would just suggest to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Labour and others who are working on that kind of an approach, that in all cases the final decisions relative to the Canadian economy should be made by the members of this House of Commons. This parliament should ratify the authority that is being considered for that consultative forum. I hope that when the Minister of Finance does decide to set a definite date to phase out controls he will be in a position to assure Canadians that he does have some measures in place to try to prevent a repetition of the kind of situation we were in as a nation, along

with others, in the summer and fall of 1975 when we implemented this program. I, along with many others who have spoken, would be happy to see the end of controls just as soon as possible. However, 1 do not believe we have arrived at that point yet.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) stated the clear case for the need for this debate when he very succinctly pointed out, as reported at page 6807 of Hansard:
There is no good time for removing controls, but this may be the best opportunity we shall have for a long time. As others have said, our production is at 80 per cent of potential, one million are unemployed, but many forces at work in the economy militate against another wage and price explosion.
In addition, it is now clear that controls, far from being the solution, are part of the problem. The government's recent paper "Agenda for Co-operation" acknowledges this situation with its somewhat vague comments on decontrol and post-controls.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in his remarks in this debate made this specific reference to food prices:
Aided by reductions in food prices at first, and the food price reduction was important and significant, the rate of price increase has come down.
He added:
It is fair to point out in connection with food prices that 60 per cent of the cost of the food going through to the consumer, at the retail level, is made up of the cost of processing, packaging, transporting and retailing, and the anti-inflation program was effective in restraining those cost increases so that the real cuts in prices were passed along to consumers.
I wish to deal specifically with those "real cuts in prices", or that other 40 per cent, that the minister suggests is the farmer-producer share of food costs. The minister and his colleagues in cabinet are suggesting the Anti-Inflation Board and the controls policy have been successful in holding down food price increases without the necessity of applying controls to primary agricultural products, which of course were excluded from the first. I suggest, however, that many farm commodity prices were effectively kept down by other means. Cattle and beef are a good example, and are the best indication that if food, notably beef, prices were indeed restrained in 1976 this restraint was at the direct expense of Canada's beef cattle industry. You might say that we, the beef producers of Canada-only about 2 per cent of the total population-gave the party. Today, half way through 1977, our total food cost is the lowest ever in terms of per capita disposable income, and you may be sure beef made a major contribution to the validity of that statement.
Let us examine some 1976 cattle and beef background facts. We reached our Canadian peak cattle population in September, 1975, and then the big cow sell down started, and extended right through all of 1976 and through the first quarter of 1977. This number reduction still continues, but at a reduced rate. It continues due to earlier severe drought conditions and general unprofitability in our cattle industry.
During the first quarter of 1976 there had been clear signs of a modest recovery in our Canadian cattle markets, with price rises of $5 to $7 per hundredweight. But for the remain-
Anti-Inflation Act
ing three quarters of 1976 disaster was allowed by this government to strike, not by action but by inaction, when a 60 per cent increase in offshore beef imports was allowed over the previous year, for a total of 188.5 million pounds. That is the equivalent of 535,000 live Canadian cows. By comparison we only marketed 600,000 Canadian cows in 1973 and 1974.
But here is the significant fact: that 60 per cent increase in offshore imports was allowed to come on to our markets on top of the largest domestic supply of beef in Canada's history. Furthermore, these imports were allowed to enter Canada at prices discounted 25 cents to 31 cents per pound below similar offshore shipments to the United States. This situation finally resulted in the infamous "six cent under rule" agreed to by industry, trade and commerce, and agriculture. That was a disgraceful sellout by the government of our beef trading rights.

speechtext:
Order, please. Leave having been granted to the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) to move the adjournment of the House pursuant to Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the clear possibility of a conspiracy concerning the concealment of evidence or the failure to take appropriate action pertaining to the

illegal break-in by three police officers at l'Agence de Presse Libre on the night of October 6-7, 1972, accordingly the motion is as follows: It is moved by Mr. Broadbent, seconded by Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre):
That this House do now adjourn.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the motion we are debating at this late hour 1 consider to be, in terms of its subject matter, one of the most serious that has ever been before the House of Commons in the history of our country.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext:
Already we are getting howls from the other side, presumably from those who are quite indifferent to the principle of the rule of law. We will see if, after my comments and those of other hon. members on this side of the House, their arrogant dismissal of that concern remains as firmly established as it is now.
The matter has two important aspects directly concerning the illegal break-in that took place at l'Agence de Presse Libre on the night of October 6-7, 1972. First it refers to "the clear possibility of a conspiracy concerning the concealment of evidence" pertaining to that break-in by three police officers. Second, it refers to "the failure to take appropriate action" concerning the same break-in. Each of these is important; each is serious.
A normal break-in in our country, that is, one by ordinary citizens of the land, is serious enough.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext: Order, please. If there are hon. members who wish to converse with each other they may want to do so behind the curtain in order to allow the hon. member to be heard.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext:
When the break-in is the result of deliberate planning and organization by Canada's police forces at every level, however-federal, provincial and municipal-it should cause every Canadian deep concern precisely because it involves the very people we hire to enforce the law, the very people who are there allegedly to protect our persons and property. Therefore my accusation about conspiracy, which was not made lightly, to conceal evidence or to fail to take appropriate action in such a serious situation, is also a matter that ought to be of deep concern to all Canadians devoted to liberty and to the principle of the rule of law in our country.
1 regret to say that the statement made today by the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) did nothing to cast doubt on the accuracy of the two-part motion which I submitted yesterday. Indeed this afternoon's statement confirmed and underlined its essential truth. I want to deal with that, Mr. Speaker.
The matter refers to the deliberate concealment of information at relevant times by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and the failure to take appropriate action when it was required by the Minister of Supply and Services at the time of the break-in in Montreal when he was solicitor general, by his
June 21, 1977

successor, and by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself. If anything is certain from the minister's speech this afternoon, it is that he has confirmed those conclusions which I originally drew from the statement the present Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) made in this House last Friday. I now want to say precisely why I feel as strongly tonight in reasserting the accuracy of the contents of that motion as I did when 1 made the motion itself.
First let me deal with the issue of concealment of evidence by the RCMP. Let me outline the scenario of events which make this conclusion inescapable.
We had the break-in on October 6-7, 1972, by three police forces in Canada; a disgraceful act. On October 10, 1972, RCMP headquarters in Ottawa were informed by the RCMP in Montreal that the RCMP had participated in this illegal break-in. Mr. Speaker, it is at this point that we get the first act of irresponsible concealment by the RCMP in Ottawa. Surely when they heard from their own office in Montreal about the violation of the Criminal Code of Canada by the RCMP it should have been brought to the attention of the minister immediately; it was not.
On October 12, 1972, the then minister of justice in Quebec, Mr. Choquette, denied in public that there was any police involvement in the break-in. He categorically said that the three policemen representing the city of Montreal, the province of Quebec and all the people of Canada in the RCMP, were not involved in that break-in. At the very time Mr. Choquette was making that public declaration, RCMP officials in Ottawa knew it was false.
It is therefore at this point that we get the second clear illustration of concealment of relevant information by the RCMP headquarters in Ottawa. They did not inform the then minister of justice of the province of Quebec that what he was saying to the people of our country was false. They did not say that the minister of justice in one of our provinces was misinforming Canadians from coast to coast about the behaviour of three of their police forces. They remained silent. Mr. Speaker, that can only be described as a conspiracy of silence. I say that seriously and, 1 think, accurately.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext:
Then, when a registered letter from the groups affected by the illegal break-in arrived at the office of the then solicitor general on October 11, it was sent off to the RCMP to be answered. After two weeks, on October 26, the RCMP sent a letter to the then executive assistant of the solicitor general recommending what can only be described as an extraordinarily irresponsible course of action: The recommendation that came to the then Solicitor General of Canada from the RCMP was that an accusation made about illegal involvement, illegal activity of the RCMP, should not even be acknowledged. Surely this is a clear dereliction of responsibility on the part of RCMP headquarters in Ottawa.
Finally at a meeting on November 6, 1972, with the minister, held to discuss the "no acknowledgement" recommendation, if I understand the purpose of that meeting, it appears
Montreal Break-In
that once again the RCMP neglected its duty. According to the then minister, and this is not refuted by the RCMP, the past commissioner of the RCMP did not even in the discussion of the letter making the accusation, tell the minister that the RCMP itself had taken part in the break-in and had indeed broken the law. That, surely, is perhaps the most shocking and disturbing culmination of a series of acts of irresponsibility.
There was a meeting with the minister to discuss a recommendation, an irresponsible recommendation which the minister did not even acknowledge. There was a letter sent by innocent Canadians making allegations about a break-in. There was in that meeting no acknowledgement by the minister himself that the RCMP was involved and had broken the law. The only qualification one can make to this last, sad statement is the claim made by Mr. Higgitt and Mr. Starnes, that they "Would be surprised if they had not verbally" advised the then solicitor general of the break-in. In passing, 1 must say 1 find it strange that neither Mr. Starnes no Mr. Higgitt can recall with greater precision whether a verbal briefing was made on this point.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext: It is a case of bad memories.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext:
Clearly, there is more than one person around with a bad memory. It seems strange to me that the statement provided by the present Solicitor General should link the two men together with an assertion that they seem to recall that it would have been normal practice for them to have briefed the minister verbally, but neither one of them remembers with a greater degree of precision whether the briefing actually took place. Surely the matter needs further investigation.
In any case, the general picture of RCMP headquarters irresponsibility concerning this break-in ought to be abundantly clear by now. They tried all along the way, from October 10 to November 2-I beg your pardon, I should have said November 6-to conceal the criminal act in which their own members were involved.
1 come now to ministerial responsibility, the second part of the matter now before the House.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext: You mean ministerial irresponsibility.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext:
I want, in discussing this point, to refer not only to the present Minister of Supply and Services, the former solicitor general, and to the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) his successor, but also to the Prime Minister. Both the Prime Minister and the present successor of the Minister of Supply and Services have been neglected in this catalogue of failure up to this point, and something needs to be said about both.
Let me begin with this point. The procedure for dealing with complaints about the RCMP is shockingly disgraceful, as was described by the present minister and his predecessors and documented in the case of the break-in at l'Agence de Presse Libre in October, 1972. The procedure illustrates in the clear-

June 21, 1977
Montreal Break-In
est possible way that, when dealing with complaints about the RCMP, we are dealing with a situation in which a person is asked to be judge of his own case, and I want to show precisely what I mean by that. The letter which arrived in the then minister's office in which an allegation was made, even if it was in the form of a question, in October, 1972, was not referred to the senior civil servants of the minister's department to be dealt with, or some other body apart from the RCMP, to be dealt with. No. As soon as the letter arrived it was shuffled off by the minister's executive assistant to the RCMP.
The letter, which was alleging the most serious kind of wrongdoing on the part of the RCMP, was sent off to the RCMP; they were to draft the reply to it. That is the procedure which existed in the then solicitor general's department for dealing with complaints about the RCMP. Surely such a procedure is basically, fundamentally wrong. That, at least, has since been admitted.
Second, I want to say something about the letter dated October 26 and sent to the then minister's executive assistant recommending, incredibly, that the solicitor general should not even acknowledge the letter sent to him by those innocent Canadians inquiring if the RCMP was involved in the break-in. Mr. Speaker, the letter of October 26 sent to the executive assistant of the then solicitor general was discussed at the meeting of November 6; and at that meeting, taking part in the discussion, was the former commissioner of the RCMP, Mr. Higgitt, and Mr. John Starnes, head of security services. Mr. Speaker, outsiders may still have reasonable grounds for doubting if the minister was told by the RCMP of their own involvement.
Unfortunately, there are still reasonable grounds for doubt, and I say this for this reason: Last December, as I said earlier today, during a long interview with a responsible reporter working for a Vancouver newspaper, the minister said he could not remember at all with precision whether he had been told. Since then his memory has sharpened and he now says clearly he remembers that he was not told. And there is some reason for fair-minded persons having doubt. However, both Mr. Starnes and Mr. Higgitt imply that there was a verbal briefing.
Indeed the current issue of Maclean's magazine which went on sale in the streets today contains a statement reportedly made by Mr. Higgitt, in which he refuses to comment on the honesty of the then solicitor general's statement. Mr. Higgitt is quoted in the issue of Maclean's magazine which went on sale in the streets today as saying, "1 don't want to deal with that," the "that" referring to the honesty of the former solicitor general's statement that he was not informed at the November 6 meeting of the break-in. I say in all seriousness that there is reason for saying that Canadians, whether in the opposition, on the government side of the House, or outside politics entirely, still have reason to doubt the statement the former solicitor general made in the House this afternoon. In any case what is beyond all doubt, in my view, is that the minister's behaviour at the time was totally inadequate in that he did not

ask the perfectly relevant, perfectly sensible question of Mr. Starnes and Mr. Higgitt at the time, namely, "Did you or did you not"-with reference to the RCMP-"take part in the raid in Montreal on the night of October 6-7, 1972?"

speechtext: It is so easy to say.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am afraid it is an important matter of judgment, and in politics we all make judgments. The minister says it is so easy to say. I am not sure it is easy to say. It is certainly a judgment which I reached. I like to think that if 1 had been in that position it would have been the most elementary, straightforward question which would have occurred to me.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext: Tough luck.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext:
I say this particularly since the minister said this afternoon that when the RCMP recommended that he should not reply to a letter which arrived in his office concerning the break-in, it was the first time he had received such a recommendation from the RCMP. If I heard his answer correctly in the House this afternoon, that is indeed what the minister said. Never before had the RCMP recommended to him that he not reply to a letter. If I got such a recommendation, particularly for the first time, it would occur to me to ask why ought 1 not to reply to the serious allegations. If nothing else prompted me to ask the question, that would have done it.
I want to go further and talk about other examples of inappropriate action or no action at all. On March 16 of last year as a result of RCMP Constable Samson's testimony, the then solicitor general, the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, learned, he said, of the break-in for the first time. Also, the Minister of Supply and Services learned of the break-in for the first time.
What did the minister of last year do when he heard that the RCMP were involved in an illegal break-in? When he heard on the basis of testimony given by an RCMP constable in court that there was illegal activity by the RCMP, what steps did the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development take?
What the minister did was offer the full co-operation of the RCMP with the Quebec inquiry which was under way into this situation. Second, he spoke to the Prime Minister and informed him of this illegal break-in. Regretfully, neither the minister nor the Prime Minister did anything else at that time of any significance. More specifically, they did not initiate a serious internal inquiry into the whole sorry situation which, as 1 have shown, reveals at best shocking neglect by the then solicitor general and cover-up action by the RCMP at the highest levels.
A year ago when the Prime Minister and the immediate past solicitor general learned of the illegal activity, they sat down with the present Minister of Supply and Services and had a chat. I am not sure what each said to the other.
June 21, 1977

The Prime Minister told me yesterday in the question period that, following the Samson revelations last March, what he did was meet with the present and former Solicitors General and did nothing else. That was as recent as yesterday's question period. Nothing that the present Solicitor General said in his presentation in the House last Friday, or in the statement this afternoon by the Minister of Supply and Services, suggests that the Prime Minister and the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development did anything more than this.
Just in case someone makes an irrelevant point that they considered a public inquiry at that time and dismissed it, I want to say that is not what I am talking about. That would have been necessary and desirable. They should have proceeded with that public inquiry. If they rejected the public inquiry for the spurious reasons given here in the last couple of days, they should have at least had an internal inquiry to find out what was wrong. They should have found out if it was at the level of former Commissioner Higgitt that a cover-up was taking place. Instead they sat out the whole process.
We have here a sad mess indeed. We have law breaking and concealment by the RCMP, an institution which Canadians from coast to coast and of every age have grown up to admire, an institution composed in the main by men and women overwhelmingly committed to honesty and decency.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext:
I would hope there would be some members on the government side who care enough about the reputation of the police forces of this country, who care enough about the principle of ministerial responsibility, who care enough about the rule of law and about the reputations of their own colleagues, individually and collectively, that they too will put aside partisanship and join us in the demand for a public inquiry which will let the facts of this case be known.
I have to say that one of the most offensive aspects of the statement on privilege made today by the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) was the cloying tribute he paid to the RCMP when he said, in effect, that he did not ask the questions he should have asked because he could not believe the RCMP would ever do such a thing. In effect the minister was saying he would speak no evil of the RCMP. He went on, being entirely consistent: he would speak no evil, his actions showed he would hear no evil, and that he would see no evil. He has brought to the House of Commons today, unfortunately supported by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), an entirely new, meaningless, and unacceptable concept of ministerial responsibility. In effect he told the House he is responsible only for what he knows, that he will go to any length at all to know as little as possible. That, Mr. Speaker, flies in the face of the principle of ministerial responsibility. It is unacceptable to the House, and it should be unacceptable to ministers and to members generally of the party opposite.

speechtext:
The leader of the New Democratic Party has reviewed most of the chronology of events but I want to address myself to some of the questions which remain to be asked.
We want to know why the minister was not advised. Was it, and this is a legitimate question, because he arranged not to be advised? Was it because the RCMP did not trust him sufficiently to advise him? Would it be the case that if we had a chance to hear the testimony of Mr. Higgitt and Mr. Starnes we would learn that he was in fact advised to a greater degree than he claims to have been advised? We do not know. We have the word of the minister. But we do not have the word of the others involved and, if the government has its way, we shall be denied the right to hear from the others who were involved and they, in turn, will be denied the right to defend themselves, to defend their reputations, to tell their part of a story which goes to the root of responsible government in this country.
The government House leader is in the Chamber and I want to pay him the tribute of making at least a passing reference to the spurious argument he raised again today, as he does so often with such great vigour whenever the government is in trouble, by suggesting that the only way in which there could be an investigation was if some member of parliament were to lay a charge. The minister well knows that the problem here is precisely that we do not have evidence on which we can lay charges. What we do have here is a situation which, on the face of it, raises questions which any responsible government would wish to be answered privately and publicly.

This matter, as the House knows, was first raised a year or more ago by my friend, the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). The government has tried consistently to cover it up, to push it aside, to avoid inquiries, to put forward its own versions by way of statements by the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox), or statements such as we heard today as to what happened. But inconvenient facts still stand out and demand explanation; sometimes taken together and sometimes singly they cry out for an inquiry.
I want to go over some of the problems which remain for all of us who are serious about the reputation of the police, about the reputation of government, about the reputation of our institutions. One of them relates to the remaining contradictions arising from just what was said at that meeting on November 6, 1972, between the then minister of supply and services, Commissioner Higgitt, and Security Services Director Starnes. Today the minister simply repeated the statements made by the Solicitor General on Friday. He categorically- that was his word-denies being told about the illegal break-in at that meeting. Neither Mr. Higgitt nor Mr. Starnes remembers telling the minister about it but, as was made clear by the Solicitor General, they do say they would be surprised if they had not done so verbally. I think it would be very difficult to conceive of a more direct way, in the circumstances, by which these two gentlemen could call into question the testimony of the then solicitor general than to use the language which was quoted by his successor in his statement on Friday.
This was, and still is, centrally, an issue of credibility. Who is right? Is it the minister who flatly denies being told, or two senior public officials who say they would be surprised if they had not told him? 1 believe this becomes more urgent in the light of the comment by Mr. Higgitt in today's Maclean's magazine that he will not deal with a question related to the veracity of the Minister of Supply and Services. We in the House of Commons, and the people generally, should be in a position to judge these questions, to judge the actions of the police. But we have no way in which to judge even the relative weight we should attach to these contradictory positions. There are no depositions, no sworn statements, no evidence under oath.
What we have is a direct statement from the Minister of Supply and Services which, it is true, is a step forward from the Solicitor General simply reporting what the Minister of Supply and Services told him. But as to Mr. Starnes' and Mr. Higgitt's version of that meeting we still have only the Solicitor General's report of what they had to say.
The Minister of Supply and Services insists, of course, that we accept his version although he and his colleagues seem determined to ensure that we shall have no opportunity to hear directly from Mr. Higgitt or from Mr. Starnes-the only way in which we can hear directly from them is through a public inquiry. By insisting that we accept his version of what took place the minister is, in effect, making very serious charges against Mr. Higgitt and Mr. Starnes. He is casting doubt upon their assertion that they would be surprised if they had not told him and, more seriously, is accusing them of a serious
June 21, 1977

dereliction of duty by failing to tell him about the break-in. They deserve the right to reply so that the whole story of what went on in that conversation and in that relationship might be heard. That is one of the inconsistencies between the positions of Mr. Higgitt and Mr. Starnes and the then solicitor general.
Another very important question which remains wide open has to do with the holes in the explanation of the Minister of Supply and Services as to why he never asked whether the RCMP had in fact engaged in an illegal break-in. By his own statements the Minister of Supply and Services admits he had had several briefings-not one, not a rare briefing, but several briefings-in regard to RCMP surveillance of the APLQ, and that he had had those briefings before the break-in. Therefore he was well aware of the interest of the force in this organization.
He also had a letter from the APLQ asking specifically whether the RCMP had been involved. Despite all that, despite his knowledge that there had been surveillance, and despite the receipt of a letter alleging involvement by the RCMP, he tells us that he never asked the most obvious question of Messrs. Higgitt and Starnes. He never even asked: "Were you gentlemen in fact involved?"
What were his reasons? He said his first reason was: "I found it hard to believe the RCMP could have participated in an illegal break-in". That is one of the most gentle ways of asking the police, of asking the public service, to carry the can for something a minister should have done.
The second reason of this minister interested in evidence was that he had seen in the press the statement by the then minister of justice of the province of Quebec, Mr. Choquette, denying any police involvement. On those very slim grounds the minister now asks us to believe that he was justified in not even asking what the RCMP, whom he knew to be investigating the APLQ, knew about the break-in.
This explanation begs another question. If the minister was so sure that the RCMP were not involved, that he did not feel any need to raise the question, why did he not respond to the letter? Surely, with all the certainty that he felt in the matter, he should have been eager to lift any suspicion from the force by giving the APLQ a flat and inequivocal answer to their inquiry. But he did not do that. What the minister is saying, then, is that he was so sure of the situation that he did not even ask. But he was not sure enough to answer a simple and direct question from the agency whose premises had been broken into.
The other matter brought out under questioning by my colleague from Central Nova this afternoon has to do with the extraordinary fact that the minister himself admitted today that this was the only occasion on which he had received instructions from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police not to answer a letter, not to act in that way. If this was such an extraordinary action, why did he not ask the simple question: "Why are you suggesting that 1 act in this way?" That is a question which is wide open and which the minister has not
Montreal Break-In
addressed. Any minister who honoured his responsibility to the people of Canada would have said: "Gentlemen, you are asking me to deviate from procedure. Why? What is going on here?" But this curiously uncurious minister did not even ask that question.
We have here as well a whole new concept of ministerial responsibility. We witnessed again this week both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Supply and Services asserting a concept of ministerial responsibility which runs completely counter to established practice under our parliamentary system. Put in its simplest form, this Goyer-Trudeau doctrine is that a minister is responsible only for those matters with which he was directly involved or had direct knowledge of. It also appears to be an implicit part of this doctrine that, on potentially embarrassing problems, ministers should go to extraordinary lengths to avoid any direct knowledge.

That is right. They do not want to be responsible ministers; they want to be bystanders so they can get out of the way when the flak comes. That makes a mockery of our parliamentary system. Only this week, in ruling that members could not direct questions on this subject to the Minister of Supply and Services, Mr. Speaker set forth as established practice the doctrine that a minister is answerable for all matters that fall under this portfolio, whether or not he knows directly about them, or indeed whether they occurred before he became the responsible minister. Ministers of the Crown just cannot have it both ways. They are quite prepared to accept responsibility for all of the positive things that government departments do. They will go forward and claim credit at the drop of a hat. But ministerial responsibility applies not just to the popular things that a government does; it applies also to the less popular and less positive things that a government does. It applies to mistakes or to errors by officials who are totally dependent upon their ministers to speak for them in parliament.
It is simply not acceptable under our system for a minister to slough off responsibility to senior officers of the RCMP. To say that he did not know and, even worse, to offer the House the lamest explanation of why he never asked, is no excuse at

all. The minister must accept responsibility for the break-in. That is what ministerial responsibility is all about. He must accept responsibility for the cover-up. tion has just exposed to the House, 1 have great respect for the Leader of the Opposition and I know he is a man who really cares for the interests of our parliamentary institutions. 1 agree with the hon. member that perhaps 1 have chosen an unusual example, but I am raising the question quite simply and I feel that maybe if the conclusion he wants to draw were carried to extremes, that comparison might be more valid than he is prepared to admit for the moment.
Mr. Speaker, of course 1 would not want to recapitulate all the facts mentioned in my statement nor the extremely concrete principles I have put forward last Friday regarding the obligation for the police forces in this country to set an extremely straightforward example and to see to it that all their actions be performed within the standards set by the law. But, I would also like to take this opportunity to point out to the House that the work of the RCMP is extremely difficult and that the RCMP absolutely needs to find again the trust of the Canadian public, which it has deserved for a very long time, it must also have again that of hon. members of this House. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, for some time now, and I say it in all sincerity, we have been witnessing far too much, in my opinion, of that process whereby hon. members come to the House with allegations, without having had the time or opportunity to check them, and throw them at us publicly, in the House of Commons. the disclosure by Corporal Samson of the break-in, but 1 will deal briefly with the Solicitor General's (Mr. Fox) arguments opposing an inquiry. Keep in mind that if this government had done its duty and examined the information available, the Quebec government would not have felt it necessary to call an inquiry. We do not object to the Quebec inquiry, for its calling is entirely consistent with the facts at the disposal of the Quebec government. The real question is, why did this government not call an inquiry before Quebec felt it necessary to call its own inquiry?
Consider what the Quebec inquiry can accomplish. The Solicitor General should have been more forthright in his response to the question asked by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). The question is, is Commissioner Higgitt a compellable witness at that hearing? Is the present Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) a compellable witness? Possibly Mr. Starnes is a compellable witness.
The issues which we in this House want to see determined cannot be determined at the Quebec inquiry, which is the biggest red herring anybody has thrown across our path tonight. Its terms of reference would not permit it to inquire into those matters we want clarified. Therefore the inquiry we want would not duplicate the Quebec inquiry.
Second, in this particular case the sentencing judge had access to documents which are probably prohibited under the doctrine of national security, and the Solicitor General has power under section 41(2) to prevent any evidence from being given before any tribunal in this country. In the Quebec case certain matters concerning national security were not made public, and the judge clearly considered them in sentencing. If necessary, at the inquiry we seek, evidence concerning national security could be heard in camera. However, we need an inquiry to examine evidence which, beyond the balance of all probability, shows there has been a cover-up.
I will not repeat past events, but it is clear that the government has abdicated its responsibility to the province of Quebec. The question arises, has it maintained the federal authority in this case? The premier of Quebec has already said he does not want the RCMP in his province, and this government has given him the best opportunity in the world for attacking the RCMP. The Solicitor General suggested that the opposition are attacking the integrity of the RCMP, but I say that this government has given the government of Quebec a terrific political lever with which to destroy the integrity of the RCMP within that province, to its everlasting shame. In the process of doing so it has helped further to fracture Canada's unity. It will have contributed substantially to the separation of that province, because one of the previous ministers concerned was guilty of sheer neglect. Probably both were guilty.
Last Friday the Solicitor General enunciated an important principle of law. Let me read what he said, as reported in Hansard, page 6795:
In a democratic society, Mr. Speaker, it is essential that those on whom, like the RCMP and the Security Service, falls the task of enforcing the law and protecting our basic liberties, can count upon the complete support of the people.

June 21, 1977
Montreal Break-In
This support, in return, must be based on the faith that those protecting these rights do themselves feel bound and indeed are bound by our laws in fulfilling their duties.
That is an excellent statement of principle, but it is typical of this government that it misses the fundamental point we are arguing. Not only must the public feel that those who enforce the laws are subject to the rule of law; they must be satisfied in a democratic society that those who enforce the laws are their servants, not their masters. We must determine if the Solicitor General maintained control of the force. He suggested we are attacking the integrity of the force, but I say its integrity is attacked every time a minister in this House becomes nothing more than an apologist for the force and does not accept ministerial responsibility for providing leadership with respect to the RCMP. And the government has dismally failed to provide it.
No police force is without its great problems. Being a policeman is a tough job. It is not a popularity contest, and there are bound to be bad policemen in any force. We say that in certain incidents the RCMP appears to have broken the law, and the minister says we are attacking the integrity of the force. But I say that we are trying to protect the integrity of the RCMP and protect the fine record and reputation of the force.
The question that is key in this matter is something else the Solicitor General said in his statement. It was in fact that the incident which occurred was neither unusual nor exceptional. I am paraphrasing. I am not saying it exactly. I point out to the Solicitor General that the evidence has been given over and over again by Corporal Ramsay, an ex-corporal in the RCMP.
I want to read some of that from tonight's paper. I hope the minister will take the trouble to have a look at it. The headline in tonight's Toronto Star reads "Break-ins Common-Former Mountie." I quote from the article:
During the last year and a half he was in the force, he said, as an assistant training officer in Saskatchewan, he was in charge of setting up classes for other officers.

The difficulty continues to be that the understanding of the present minister and his two predecessors of the role of Solicitor General is that it is

simply to protect and apologize for any activity of those in the force or in the bureaucracy that they represent. The Canadian people are really getting a little tired of it.
There is a rule of political leadership in a democratic society that the RCMP must, above all other people, surely obey the law. However, the Canadian public are in doubt right now that the political authorities are in control of the force. On that point alone I plead with the government to call an inquiry into this specific matter even if it does not wish to expand it into the others I am going to suggest also cry out for an inquiry.
I am not critical of the present Minister of Supply and Services in terms of his handling of the matter in the House this afternoon. I think he made a forthright statement. It was something he was not required to do under the rules. I am not critical of the present minister for the statement that he made in the House. But, as many people have pointed out, that statement raises far more questions than it answers.
However, what is important are two things that the minister, in answer to the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), inserted in the record. One of them perhaps goes to the root of the problem. He said "that is easy to say", in response to the question of whether he should have asked the key question following the November 6 meeting.
Hindsight is very easy. The fact that he did not ask the key question goes beyond what was negligence of his part. It goes to the root of the question as to whether he understands the role of Solicitor General to be more than an apologist, to have a positive obligation, to find out whether in fact the force is obeying the law of the country. It is that duty the solicitor general at the time failed to meet.
Sure, hindsight is easy, but it is not just a question of negligence. It is a failure of this government's understanding of its role with respect to the RCMP because it did not occur to the minister to ask a question. He still sees his role as being the protector of the force. He would never believe they would break the law. That is at the root of the minister's failure. I am not challenging the veracity of the statement that the minister made, although it certainly raises some question of judgment.
The other line that the minister threw into debate, and I will be pleased to listen to his further comments, was to call this back-seat driving on the part of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, I say to the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that it is better to have somebody driving even if it is in the back seat, because what we have had was that no one who had that particular portfolio did any driving. He was being driven by the force and being ignored by the force.
In the United States a president was impeached because three operatives, not police officers, broke into the Watergate complex. The only reason we are debating this in the House today is because an RCMP corporal who was charged in an illegal bombing let slip in the evidence that he participated in a break-in. Otherwise there would never have been this debate in the House of Commons today. This matter would never have come to light.
June 21, 1977

The facts are obvious about a cover-up. The logic is overwhelming that there was a cover-up. Democracy cannot survive that kind of conduct. We need to have a complete and open society. The only way the government can demonstrate that it is in favour of that, and I plead with it tonight, is to agree to have an inquiry into this matter. It will be the first step back to restoring the integrity of the RCMP and putting ministerial responsibility where it belongs.
This is a serious time. 1 will not deal with the Praxis question because my time is limited. However, there are some serious questions with regard to that which remain unanswered. I will throw the name of Letourneau into this debate and 1 will deal more with that. This is another question of illegality on the part of the RCMP in Quebec. There was the Royal American show, the illegal police bugging. The police investigation in that case was simply to call in the officers, ask whether they did it, and when the officers said no, they said that was fine. Can you imagine an ordinary citizen alleged to have committed an offence being treated in that way? No statement was required and there was no investigation. Further evidence has now come out of that.
There is the New Brunswick inquiry, again the question of RCMP responsibility. There is now so much cumulative evidence that we have to start to redress on that balance.
When 1 began practising law the courts were very scrupulous, very careful that the rule of law was always obeyed. 1 am afraid there has been a swing in the pendulum. Because of a deep concern about rising crime, we have started to cut corners to control it. That is a great mistake. The kind of civilized and free society that we have cannot exist if we do not have a government which understands that the people are the masters of the RCMP and must remain so.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have listened to the discussion of the APLQ incident for the past two days and I am shocked by the lack of rigour, discipline and the degree of irresponsibility with which opposition members have carried on, making gratuitous allegations and insinuations.
What is the opposition after-the truth or sensationalized press reports? The opposition parties are so miserably lacking in creative ideas and policy proposals that I can understand this might be the only way for them to obtain press coverage. However, parliamentary tradition suggests that if any member chooses to argue on the basis of allegations and insinuations he should have enough courage, enough guts, to specify his accusations and to put his job on the line to prove them. I have already said 1 would put my seat on the line to support my statements.
For example, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has insinuated that I may have misled the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) in my account of the facts concerning my involvement in this incident. If he wants to accuse me of concealing evidence, let him be specific about it and let him pay the price if he fails to prove his accusation. If he chooses not to put up, he should
Montreal Break-In
shut up. The Leader of the Opposition is of course hesitant to stake his seat, because he knows very well that these allegations are unfounded.
As for some other members of the opposition, unfortunately they have not behaved very responsibly, either. Their tactics were clear: insinuation and innuendo. They obviously did not pay attention to the Solicitor General's statement. They chose to extract only those parts of the statement which suited their purpose. They chose to conveniently overlook important pieces of information.
One member was unethical and irresponsible enough to accuse me of having been involved in three "scandals". He should have more respect for the English language and use such words as "scandal" more judiciously. He should have enough respect for individual rights and reputations to use such words more carefully. First, though the purchase of aircraft from the Lockheed Corporation did give rise to serious problems, in no way could the negotiations be qualified as scandalous. We all know how hard the opposition tried to uncover a scandal, to no avail.
The second incident referred to by the member is the Hamilton dredging incident. I would like to correct an erroneous news report published as a result of the statement made by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) concerning my alleged involvement in the Hamilton dredging incident.
The members's allegations are false. This incident was dealt with in parliamentary committee which unequivocally concluded that I had acted correctly and responsibly in dealing with this matter. Furthermore I am tabling, with the signator's consent and, I hope, with the consent of the House, a letter sent to me by Mr. James E. Campbell, then Controller, City of Hamilton, dated April 8, 1975, which should erase any doubts which anyone might have concerning my role in this incident. It reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Goyer:
I felt that 1 should write to you as a result of the vicarious exchanges between us reported by the news media.
The news media and others were quick to seize upon and exploit a statement by me that certain information was handed to you when what was meant was that it was handed to your office.
At any rate the matter was acted upon swiftly as reported in the Globe and Mail on or about December 14, 1972 in a report that the RCMP had commenced an investigation of Hamilton Harbour.
If I can be of any help to correct any statement that may have caused any embarrassment to you or your department, I would be pleased to do so.
Yours truly,
James E. Campbell Controller

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext:
At the risk of repeating my earlier statement, I will explain my role in the APLQ incident once again. The Solicitor General has already tabled a statement; L myself, have risen on a question of privilege to explain my role in this incident; I trust that, the third time around, opposition mem-

June 21, 1977
Montreal Break-In
bers will begin to grasp the facts. I sympathize with the many opposition members who are just plain slow at grasping issues, but those who refuse to grasp the facts, who distort the truth are abusing their position as members of parliament and are abusing the confidence of their electors.
First, I want to state flatly that 1 had no prior knowledge of the October 6/7 1972 break-in at the APLQ. The Solicitor General has also stated that neither the RCMP Headquarters in Ottawa nor the Commanding Officer of "C" Division in Montreal had been told of the break-in prior to the operation being carried out.
Second, a letter dated October 9 was sent to me by the APLQ. The letter did not state that the RCMP had participated in the break-in, it asked if it had. This letter, received October 11, 1972, was not immediately brought to my attention but was referred to the RCMP. This was standard practice, and this afternoon I explained that practice.
As 1 mentioned this afternoon, this method of dealing with complaints about the RCMP was not ideal, but those were the tools available to me at the time. And in the early fall of 1972, 1 had recommended to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that a commission be instituted to look into disciplinary questions and the manner of dealing with complaints about RCMP behaviour. The commission was in fact established by my successor.
On October 26, 1972, the RCMP wrote to my assistant recommending that no acknowledgment of the letter be sent, without providing the reason for their recommendation.
My agenda indicates that 1 would have raised the matter with the Commissioner and the Director of Security Services of the RCMP on November 6, 1972. I was not informed of RCMP involvement in the break-in at this meeting nor at any subsequent meeting with the police. I was advised not to acknowledge the letter because the theft of documents referred to in the APLQ letter fell under the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities and 1 was informed that la Police de Montreal was investigating the incident.
1 am sure that 1 was not told of RCMP involvement in the break-in. The former Commissioner and former Director of Security Services claim they would be surprised if they had not told me verbally. But, neither the Commissioner nor the Director of Security Services of the RCMP remember actually telling me about RCMP involvement in the incident. They both state that the matter was a very serious one and very unusual. Do you not think, Mr. Speaker, they would remember discussing it with me? Do you not think that had they wanted to inform me about it they would have done so in writing?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ALLEGED COVER-UP OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext:
The RCMP's standard way of dealing with important information was to convey it to me in writing. I outlined the procedure this afternoon, but let me repeat that many days 1 received up to five or six documents on police matters. Decisions and policy directives were recorded in writing and such documents were initialled by me. The RCMP

is methodical, efficient, and thorough in keeping its records of discussions and decisions. The Solicitor General Department's files and those of the RCMP contain no written report to me on the APLQ break-in.
Why did 1 not specifically ask if the RCMP was involved in the break-in? First 1 received an inquiry about an illegal break-in from a group whose reputation and credibility hon. members can evaluate themselves. I found it hard to believe that the RCMP could have participated in an illegal break-in. 1 had no knowledge of the RCMP ever having taken part or even having planned to take part in illegal activities. I respected the RCMP's reputation and past record. The opposition is being cynical and opportunistic when they wonder why I trusted the RCMP. They were the ones, especially Tory members, who were attacking me at the time for not showing enough respect for the RCMP.
Secondly, when 1 discussed the APLQ letter with the RCMP, the Quebec justice minister had already stated publicly that no police force was involved in the break-in. He had prime responsibility for investigating the incident; he had done so and was unequivocal in his conclusion. Was it reasonable for me to doubt his conclusions? The RCMP did not tell me of RCMP involvement in the break-in, the Quebec justice minister stated bluntly that no police force was involved; it was thus clear to me that the RCMP was not involved in the incident. I had no reason to suspect the conclusions of the Quebec minister of justice as false and thus no reason to ask the RCMP if they had been involved in the incident. No member of this House would have reacted differently. When I was also told that the whole matter was being further investigated by the Montreal urban police, I was further reassured that justice would take its course.
The Quebec justice minister's statement denying that any of the three police forces were involved in the theft of documents was never brought to my attention as false.
On November 27, 1972, I was appointed Minister of Supply and Services, and the very first time 1 learned of RCMP involvement in the break-in was in March 1976.
As I pointed out this afternoon, neither the deputy solicitor general nor the then director, security planning and research group, were made aware of RCMP participation in this operation before March 16, 1976. The established practice called for their being informed of important questions pertaining to the RCMP's activities, to allow them to assist me in following up on such matters. Normally, at least one of them attended my meetings with the police. Neither one remembers even hearing about RCMP involvement in the break-in at the APLQ.
This now brings me to the broader question of the role and duties of a solicitor general as they pertain to responsibility for the RCMP. First of all, in a democratic society, day-to-day police operations should be carried out as independently as possible from the political process and the police should not be used to further political aims. As Solicitor General I was under severe pressure from opposition members not to involve myself
June 21, 1977

in the day-to-day operations of the force; opposition members watched carefully to ensure that I was not interfering with police operations.
1 agree that with regard to specific day-to-day police operations the role of the Solicitor General should be non-intrusive unless of course there is proof that police conduct is unworthy or illegal. 1 can assure the House that when 1 was Solicitor General, the RCMP was never asked to undertake any activities to further political interests nor was I ever made aware of any illegal police activities, under any circumstances. Thus my actions toward the RCMP were directed at policy matters at finding ways and means to make the RCMP even more effective and efficient.
Let me give the House some examples of how this was done. First of all, the whole recruiting process was reviewed, with special attention being given to upgraded entrance requirements. Bilingualism and multilingualism combined to make the force more representative of Canadian society and more efficient. It was decided that women could become members of the force. A national committee, formed of members of the force, was established to discuss problems and issues relating to improving conditions and relations between the commissioner and members of the force, and thus improving the work environment. 1 recommended the establishment of a commission to deal with disciplinary questions and the manner in which to deal with complaints about RCMP behaviour. A public relations program focusing on crime prevention was established in numerous schools throughout the country.
Some of the RCMP's methods of operation were reviewed and discontinued. For example, I put an end to the practice of soliciting information from young informers. 1 encouraged the RCMP to put added emphasis on white collar crime.
Of course, 1 also paid a great deal of attention to national security problems. That is what a Solicitor General should do. Threats to our national security arise not only from outside our borders but also from within the country itself. We had had bombings; innocent persons had been maimed and killed; political kidnappings and murder had taken place. It is easy for a member of the opposition to accuse me of "paranoia" about terrorist groups, but then what does this member know about national security? In fact, because I knew that members of the opposition parties knew very little about national security matters, I undertook, for the first time, to have the then leader of opposition briefed about security issues.
I repeat what I said this afternoon. No matter what I had been told about the APLQ's activities, under no circumstances would I have authorized an illegal break-in at the premises of the APLQ if I had had any prior knowledge of the operation. Had I been told about RCMP involvement in the break-in, under no circumstances would I have condoned it or covered up for the force. No circumstances can serve as an excuse for illegal behaviour not even with the best of intentions.
I have spent a good part of my life defending individual rights and civil liberties-as a student, as a private citizen, as a politician. If anything, I have been accused of being too staunch a supporter of individual rights. I was not naive,
Montreal Break-In
however, in my support of individual rights and collective freedom; 1 took national security questions very seriously, seriously enough to show prudence, seriously enough not to condone illegal police activities.
In order to get a better grasp of security matters, I established the Security Planning and Research Group to assist me in analyzing the great volume of material passed on to me by the security services of the RCMP. The SPARG was designed to advise me on policy matters, not to engage in police operations. It is just impossible for the Solicitor General to analyse closely the masses of information conveyed to him by the security services of the RCMP. He does not have the time and all the expertise to do so. The SPARG worked in close co-operation with the security services of the RCMP, and in the final months of my mandate had also begun to link with the Commissioner of the RCMP becoming more involved in studying other types of police information.
When I established the SPARG, however, I was severely attacked by opposition members for setting up a group that would, in effect, review and analyze some of the material provided to me by the RCMP.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to table the letter I quoted from.

The opposition claimed the RCMP was very capable of reviewing its information itself, that no independent analysis was required, that I was threatening the independence of the force. It is ironic that now the opposition is conveniently accusing me of not having intervened enough in police operations.
I feel that I did a good job in dealing with the RCMP- improved recruiting standards, better employer relations mechanisms, a review of disciplinary issues, the abolition of certain questionable operations, namely, those pertaining to young informers, a renewed emphasis on white collar crimes, an increased emphasis on crime prevention, a more effective security service. I did not know that the RCMP was involved in the APLQ incident before, during or after the break-in.

June 21, 1977
Montreal Break-In
One final comment: some members and journalists have tried to link this incident to the Watergate affair which occured in the United States. 1 wonder why Canadians are always so eager to emulate slavishly the United States? First of all, any comparison with the Watergate incident is so far-fetched that it is flabbergasting that anyone would waste his time attempting to make such a comparison. The Watergate incident involved the hiring of a group of men to take part in an illegal break-in and bugging of a recognized political party, for political purposes.
Various senior members of the U.S. administration had prior knowledge of the break-in, at least a few days after it had occured; senior members of the administration admitted trying to "pay off' the burglars to buy their silence, and in fact tried to cover up the whole matter. The APLQ incident is very, very different. First, no senior RCMP officers, no federal minister had prior knowledge of the break-in. No one was hired to do the job. The APLQ cannot justly be compared to the Democratic Party and, moreover, no political motive was involved. I was not informed of RCMP involvement in the incident; the Prime Minister was certainly not aware of the matter. No one was paid to keep his mouth shut. No minister was involved in a cover-up; on the contrary, as soon as a minister was in fact informed of RCMP participation in the break-in, an investigation was launched and charges were laid. One would have to have a very vivid and warped imagination to call this a "Watergate".
On the other hand it is obvious, given the nature of the debate which has taken place here, that members of the opposition have relied more on their imagination than on facts. Hopefully, their future statements will reflect more accurately what really happened.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am almost ashamed to take part in this debate following the former solicitor general, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), a man who hears no evil, sees no evil, and speaks no evil. Seldom are we treated to such a sanctimonious performance and contribution as we heard tonight in the House.
The Minister said on several occasions today that he is willing to lay his job on the line if some hon. members made some charges and some accusations. 1 want to try to oblige this gentleman, who speaks with a squeaky voice, to see if I can arouse the minister's sensivity sufficiently to do what he promised, namely, stand up and resign his seat.
In 1973 the former great prime minister, Lester B. Pearson, said that if our security policy ignored or did not take into account the basic rights of the individual, it could operate not to defend but to destroy the liberties which were our first concern.
In February of 1974 our present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said, making reference to the security service, that the public security service is the custodian of part of the independence which every citizen yields so that the state may

act with the necessary authority for the common good. He referred to this assumed mandate as a sacred trust. This was the very language that every despot who wished in the past to curb or destroy the rights of citizens employed. Given the lack of parliamentary control over the nation's security system and the Prime Minister's known predilection for conducting political vendettas for the benefit of Liberals, what assurance is there that the security measures are not simply a political weapon?
The Solicitor General calls his actions or the goings on in connection with the APLQ a very unusual and serious incident. He says the reason no action was taken in the case of Montreal was because it was a very isolated incident. But apart from the break-in at L'Agence de Presse Libre du Quebec, we have heard about investigations in similar instances in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. There is also the case of Katie Curtin and Sylvia Roche who were fired from their jobs at the Olympic Games in July, 1976, along with many others who were fired for security reasons. The reason I mention that case is that the lieutenant in the cross-examination by the Montreal police which investigated that incident said that Curtin and Roche were on the list of persons who were considered to be security risks. Corp. Gerard Lafond of the Quebec provincial police admitted at the same hearing that hundreds of files are maintained on persons who have never been arrested or charged, on persons who are suspected of being security risks. According to his testimony, duplicate copies were maintained by the RCMP.
I would like to deal first with some of the actors in this drama which is unfolding here tonight and has been unfolding in the last few days. First I will throw out a few names. There is the name of the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), and the name of Lt. Col. Bourne who was involved, as we know, during the war measures crisis, in the Prime Minister's office dealing with some of the troubles in Quebec. There are the names of Starnes, Dabros, Cobb, all people who came from various offices such as the Department of National Defence, the Privy Council office, the Prime Minister's office and the RCMP forces. They brought with them the mentality of the War Measures Act and the October crisis in Quebec. There was a communist behind every tree, there was a leftist everywhere, and we were all nervous. Eyes were looking out of every mail box.

speechtext:
The present Minister of Supply and Services came to his position in the Prime Minister's office after having been parliamentary assistant to the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Sharp). Lt. Col. Robin Bourne was already doing security work in the Privy Council office and he linked up with the Minister of Supply and Services. Col. Walter Dabros was fresh from the battle grounds where he was fighting subversives on the campuses, and he brought his experience to this select group, insp. Cobb did FLQ work in Quebec from August, 1966, to June, 1970. This group now became the custodians of
June 21, 1977

the independence we had to yield as Canadians to the government so that the state could protect the common good.
Now 1 want to speak about yet another break-in, another crime that was committed in support of the public good, that is, the crime that was committed during the break-in in the late 1970's in the office of the Praxis Corporation in Toronto. That group could be identified a little better. It was a group of individuals who formed a social action group. They came into this environment in response to the call for a just society, for participatory democracy. They were operating on grants, one particular grant given to them by the National Council on Social Welfare to organize a poor peoples' conference. They played their part in the grant economy of the late 1960's, encouraged of course by the Prime Minister who was going to make everybody equal and everybody happy.
They were called leftist because they were working with the poor people, getting them to participate, which the Prime Minister wanted them to do with the taxpayers' money. This same philosophy gave rise to rifling groups as well, some of them very radical. There were small vigilante groups operating at that time. The police, of course, aligned itself with right wing groups. In the case of Praxis one did not need to be a member of the RCMP to act under the protection of 141(2) which gives the minister the right to withhold evidence from the courts. All one needed to be was to be a member of one of these right wing groups, and as such one was granted immunity from the law. This is what happened in the case of the Praxis break-in.
It would appear that in the Praxis case there might not have been a direct involvement of a police force. In fact the government did not investigate this action as it did the case in Montreal, but our own investigation reveals that the police might have acted through agents, and one agent in particular who is no longer in the country. His life would have been in danger if the police had revealed his identity on January 24 when I introduced the black list in the House. It is now seven years after the event, but this person's life would still be in danger today. I ask myself who would do harm, shoot or kill this person who co-operated with the police at that time? Would it be the RCMP who would do it to conceal their involvement? Would it be a leftist or a rightist group? What kind of a society do we live in today when a person who collaborates with the police is in danger of his life?
Supt. Venner of the RCMP met the people who lost their files in the break-in. When the question of the obstruction of the investigative process of the Metro police by the RCMP was raised, Supt. Venner said:
Yes, we found ourselves in a dilemma of protecting this person. This was unfair to the Metro police but there was nothing we could do. If we gave out names, that would have put this anonymous person in danger.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) knows what happened.
