The simple conclusion one can reach with respect to this matter has two aspects. First, all along during the course of the questioning there was a resistence and a repugnance on the part of the government with respect to questions raised by opposition members as to the circumstances, the background, and the ministerial involvement concerning the break-in at L'Agence de Presse Libre du Quebec.
Only this month the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) attempted to split hairs and suggest to the House without equivocation that the Minister of Supply and Services, the then solicitor general, had absolutely no knowledge that the RCMP were involved because the letter which was sent to his office only referred to police. It was subsequently pointed out to the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General that there was no simple deduction which could be made by the Prime Minister on the basis of his discussions with the Minister of Supply and Services. That was because there was a telegram attached to that letter. It was addressed to the Assistant Commissioner of the RCMP in Montreal. It specifically asked about their involvement and thereby implicated the RCMP.
Then we have the Solicitor General telling us in his prepared statement that he is satisfied that the Minister of Supply and Services knew nothing until March of 1976, based on his investigation. In the next paragraph he has the audacity and temerity to point out the fact that there was a discussion and a consideration by the Minister of Supply and Services with respect to the allegation of the illegal break-in of the APLQ directly after that break-in. The Minister of Supply and Services answered tonight that he could not believe this particular proposition. The combination of that peculiar logic and rationale stretches our incredulity. If you combine with that the attempt of everyone in the government to make us believe that there was no knowledge of any RCMP involvement, it cries out for an independent inquiry into this whole proposition. The suggestions made by hon. members on this side are justifiable and should be acted upon.
The Solicitor General has made reference to the Quebec inquiry. He made a suggestion that the Alberta situation was somehow similar. There is a very, very important distinction in that situation because in Alberta there is no involvement of a cabinet minister. In this particular case it is not only a question of RCMP involvement, of wrongdoing, and a possibility of cover-up in the senior echelons after being told of the illegal break-in, but the instance extends directly to the doorstep of the Minister of Supply and Services.
The Minister of Supply and Services takes exception to my statement in this House, which I do not retract one bit. In my experience in this House of Commons since 1974 this man has been involved in three scandalous instances. The word "scandal" covers a wide sector of inappropriate, incompetent, and wrongful acts, in my view. We were involved in an explanation by the Minister of Supply and Services with respect to the Hamilton Harbourgate matter for which he bears no responsibility because his office staff failed to communicate the information received from the Controller in Hamilton. Next we had the Lockheed procurement situation. What is not scandalous

about a billion dollar contract which is not reduced to writing in a department responsible for that particular transaction? Probably that was the only thing which preoccupied him in that department. Finally, we have an admitted illegality with respect to the RCMP break-in of the APLQ.
In each case the Minister of Supply and Services has used the same device. He does not accept responsibility for what has transpired. He sloughs off the blame. In this case he blamed the RCMP; he has blamed his executive assistant; and he has fired Larry Stopforth. The same pattern always develops every time this man gets into trouble, and now he is telling us to accept that he was not guilty of any act of commission or omission. As far as our party is concerned, that is not acceptable.
As far as I am concerned, if the government fails to take steps to have an inquiry with respect to this incident, there will be an outcry from the people of Canada that the government will hear for some time to come.

Mr. Speaker, 1 have one or two brief comments to make. I find it somewhat regrettable to have to rise this evening to level accusations having listened to the personal defence statements of prominent members of the government in recent weeks, recent months. I have listened to them trying to rationalize their positions with respect to matters that are of concern to the Canadian public.
I rise to pose at the close of this debate one primary question, and I direct it to the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) who has had the courtesy to remain in his seat after one who used to be a very dear friend, and I hope who is still an honourable friend, has left the Chamber. 1 hope he left the Chamber because he was tired at 2.15 in the morning. I rise to ask a primary question on the responsibility of the government in using acts of parliament respecting the Canadian military in pursuit of information, the use of the Canadian Armed Forces which, as we all know, is our primary force of security, and the use of the military in terms of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
In recent years we have indirectly done an enormous injustice to the RCMP as a result of the improper use of what the government considers to be its requirements with respect to security and intelligence information.
I had no intention of entering this debate at all. It is outside of my competence, but it is not outside of my knowledge as regards the degree to which the government over the years had used, deliberately and with malicious intent, its powers to affect the reputation of the RCMP and its internal security investigation capacities. It has maligned the reputation of the force in the eyes of the public to such a degree that the press today accuses us of being anti-RCMP.

I am speaking of the degree to which the Solicitor General and his predecessors have acquiesced in the abuse of national trust by directions which have removed cabinet from public responsibility. I think that this is what many of us object to, and if the Solicitor General is not aware of what I am talking about he should apprise himself of the degree to which the military, the PMO and internal security devices have been used to direct the RCMP to do certain work for him. He should apprise himself of the damage that he and his colleagues are doing. 1 suggest he do that, because only then can we come to some rationalization of what is taking place. So over-zealous is he about the rights of Canadians that he has allowed the abuse to result in accusations. I suggest that the Solicitor General apprise himself of the facts, and if he does know what is going on in terms of his internal security, and 1 suspect he does not-

I suspect he does not. 1 ask him this because I have some respect for him; at least I have had it up to this point in time. Perhaps after this evening I will have to review that conclusion. I suggest that he apprise himself thoroughly of what went on before he joined the august ranks of the Treasury benches of this government which he supports. Let him find out what has been done in the name of justice as perceived by his leader. Let him find out about the misadventures that have been blamed upon the national police force of this country that have been perpetrated by directions, through other security analysis groups, to the RCMP, the extent to which the RCMP has been used by other forces. 1 think he has the capacity to apprise himself of these facts, and if he does not he will be a disappointment not only to his own colleagues on the back benches.
1 do not know what the Solicitor General's gesture means. If he cares to stand up and tell me, we can go on to discuss it for the next two or three hours. I suggest that the gestures of the Solicitor General are rather meaningless.
The point 1 am trying to make is that I reject and react against the degree to which the Canadian military has been used to direct our national police force in the types of involvements that it has become engrossed with in recent years. As far as 1 am concerned successive solicitors general have denied that, for example, the telephones of members of parliament have ever been tapped. It would be a curious spectacle to see the Solicitor General stand in his place now on a question of privilege or on a point of order and deny that that has ever happened, because it would give me great delight to demonstrate to him that he would not know what he was talking about if he were to deny it. It would give me even greater delight to expose the fraud and the nonsense that I have listened to for the last ten or 12 years from successive solicitors general with respect to these questions.
I have been lied to in this House by ministers of the Crown when they, to my knowledge, have had explicit facts in front of

them with respect to the truth. Therefore we can hardly be faulted for being skeptical with respect to some of the responses we have received from the other side of the Chamber this evening. The motion, which is in front of us, is a very serious one.
The Solicitor General is still here. I doubt very much that he is still here because of respect for parliament. I suspect, rather, that he is here because the great sacrifice is worth it, because he can sit and laugh at people who rise in their places to express grievous concern about the arrogance of the government and the extent to which the government opposite has gone to subvert rights in this country that many of us hold to be very valid and very true. Without the protection of these rights this country will not survive. I think the minister knows of what I am speaking.
Sometimes we talk at great length and in great circles without bothering to talk about what in fact is bothering us. It has bothered me for many years that the government has deliberately set out to establish a system of virtual espionage. The government condones it and finds ways of removing itself from direct responsibility, and its members sit in their places early in the morning and laugh and chuckle at what are in fact very grave matters with respect to the capacity of Canadians to continue to believe in the proposition that the central government should remain strong in this country, and 1 wonder sometimes about the smiles and the arrogance of knowing that there are those of us on this side who do know differently and yet who, for a variety of reasons, are not permitted to speak out.
I come back to my essential point. As the new Solicitor General goes forward and becomes well established and well accepted in his position, he should be conscious and continue to be aware of the concerns some Canadians have about the impact that he can have with respect to decisions taken by the government he supports, and with respect to the grave influence that he has on the security and intelligence work of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and of elements of the Canadian Armed Forces today. I reject the minister's smile because I have been one of those who have been subjected to exactly that influence.
If the Solicitor General is curious, I shall give him a hint so that he can narrow his search. This goes back to the days when we were debating in this House a peculiar piece of legislation called the Canadian Forces Reorganization Act in 1965-66. It was not yesterday, but it was not too long ago either. The progressive degree to which the government, for some pathological reason not discernible to most Canadians, bothers to go to the trouble to direct the Canadian military to overtake, 1 suggest, and direct the security intelligence work of the national police force, is a matter of some concern to at least some of us in this Chamber, and 1 hope the Solicitor General can suppress his smiles and giggles in this respect.

Sooner or later the government has got to be told to wake up and be aware. There are those of us in this country who reject the presence of the Canadian Armed Forces in our penitentiaries, for example, for the purposes of quelling riots, or for the purpose of serving one social will over another. If that is the acceptable thing, then we should change the role of the Canadian military in our society and our structure. But we should do it openly and do it through dialogue.
I think this is an appropriate time to say these things. It is early in the morning. There is probably nobody in the press gallery. There are certainly very few people in the public galleries.
Obviously there is nobody here of any great consequence. Prosper keeps lecturing us. The Solicitor General keeps smiling. The distinguished sailor from Saskatchewan, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), for whom 1 have great personal respect, keeps smiling.
In conclusion, we must be very careful in our inner circles, in our very private circles, in our very inner sanctoriums, or whatever they are called, where we make public decisions, that we do not remove our capacity to get at decisions about the security of our country and the methods by which we continue to ensure that the security of our country is under control or in good hands. We must be very careful about the degree to which we use the Canadian military in that pursuit because, to the degree that we do, we impair national unity in the final analysis. This does not enhance it.
I should like to give a scenario or two for the Solicitor General but might come dangerously close to saying things I should not. However, 1 am sufficiently concerned about the debates of the last two or three years to say to the minister that I deplore the degree to which he has impaired the reputation and the capacity of our national police force to be an effective security and intelligence group within our nation.

Perhaps I could then put two or three rhetorical questions that the minister or any member of the government might answer. They were not answered during the debate.
One of the distressing aspects of this is that so much of the government's case has centered upon the fact that the former solicitor general felt it should be self-evident that it was not necessary to reply to the letter he received requesting information about whether the RCMP had been involved in the break-in. He indicated that any member of the House would have reacted in the same way. According to the statement made by the present Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) last Friday, however, the letter was sent to the former solicitor general on October 11, 1972. It was brought to the attention of the RCMP by the assistant to the minister, Lieutenant Colonel John R. Cameron, in order that a reply could be prepared for the solicitor general's signature.
After that letter was sent to the RCMP on October 26, 1972, the RCMP wrote to the minister's assistant recommending that no acknowledgment be made, without providing reasons for that recommendation. The question I should like to leave in the air this evening, and perhaps pursue at a later date with the minister, is whether he has personally seen that exchange of correspondence between the assistant to the solicitor general and the RCMP. I note that the minister nods his head in assent. If he has seen it, would he be prepared to inform the House who the official was who signed the letter to the then solicitor general on behalf of the RCMP, recommending that no reply be made to the letter to the solicitor general?
Next, I wonder if the Solicitor General would be prepared to bring copies of the correspondence to the House tomorrow to be tabled so that it would be on the public record.
The reason this information is so important is that each of us receives correspondence from individuals and organizations every day. There may be instances when we feel it is improper for us to give a complete reply to questions asked, perhaps because matters are before the courts or we do not have the relevant information. As a matter of procedure, however, virtually any member would at least do any individual or group who wrote the courtesy of explaining why an answer would not be forthcoming.
If, as the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) indicated, the reason he did not write was that the Minister of Justice in Quebec, Mr. Choquette, had stated publicly that the RCMP was not involved and that he accepted Mr. Choquette's statement, I would be curious to know why he did not write back to the organization and say that the Minister of Justice in Quebec had looked into the matter and determined there was no involvement by the federal police force and that he could answer categorically that that was not the case. If his concern

It would also allow us to pursue further questions on what degree of knowledge there was within the RCMP, and what participation there was in suppressing information about the illegal break-in.
